    #227600. Tech Report: Protecting Attorney-Client Relationships: ABA advocacy helps safeguard the right to effective assistance of counsel

    📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (921 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Protecting Attorney-Client Relationships: ABA advocacy helps safeguard the right to effective assistance of counsel

    📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Attorney-client privilege, the lawyer’s ethical duty of confidentiality and the U.S.
    • According to recent reports, to defend these principles and ensure lawyers can continue to represent their clients effectively, the ABA actively engages with Congress and federal agencies based on its long-standing policies passed by its House of Delegates.
    • In 2022 and 2024, the ABA helped defeat the Enablers Act, which would have harmed many lawyers and law firms by regulating them as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act and requiring them to report extensive attorney-client privileged and other protected client information to the government.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Attorney-client privilege, the lawyer’s ethical duty of confidentiality and the U.S. Constitution’s right to the effective assistance of counsel are bedrock legal principles that encourage clients to speak candidly with their lawyers without fear the information they share will be revealed to others. This enables clients to receive the most competent legal advice possible from fully informed counsel.

    According to recent reports, to defend these principles and ensure lawyers can continue to represent their clients effectively, the ABA actively engages with Congress and federal agencies based on its long-standing policies passed by its House of Delegates. In the past decade, the association’s advocacy has resulted in significant successes, and the ABA continues to oppose various measures requiring lawyers to disclose protected client information. Recent examples illustrate the breadth of the ABA’s advocacy.

    In 2022 and 2024, the ABA helped defeat the Enablers Act, which would have harmed many lawyers and law firms by regulating them as financial institutions under the Bank Secrecy Act and requiring them to report extensive attorney-client privileged and other protected client information to the government.

    According to recent reports, the ABA also helped to reverse the “persuader” rule adopted by the Labor Department that would have required many lawyers and law firms representing employers to report confidential client information to the government. A federal court struck down the new rule in 2016, and the Labor Department rescinded it two years later based in part on comments submitted by the ABA. The ABA continues to oppose legislative efforts to reinstate the rule, including the Protecting the Right to Organize Act of 2021, which has been reintroduced in each Congress since then.

    In a recent development, the ABA’s advocacy produced another important result when U.S. Customs and Border Protection adopted a new policy in 2018 in response to concerns raised by the ABA. The new policy substantially increased protections for privileged and other confidential client information on lawyers’ laptops, cellphones and other electronic devices during border crossings.

    Recent findings suggest that more recently, the ABA helped persuade the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to formally withdraw its proposed “duty of candor” rule, which would have imposed new regulations on many lawyers representing clients before FERC and required them to disclose confidential client information to the agency. The ABA submitted comments to FERC in 2022 urging it not to apply the rule to lawyers representing clients because it would undermine the authority of the state supreme courts and weaken both the attorney-client privilege and the confidential lawyer-client relationship. In November 2025, FERC announced that based on the comments from the ABA and other stakeholders, it was withdrawing the proposal and terminating the rulemaking proceeding.

    The ABA is currently working with the Treasury Department in an attempt to persuade the Financial Action Task Force to prepare a favorable mutual evaluation report on the United States’ efforts to combat money laundering. The FATF, the global standard-setting body, is preparing the report to determine whether U.S. laws, regulations and other measures relating to its financial institutions, lawyers and law firms, and other key sectors comply with current FATF standards or whether upcoming U.S. regulations are needed.

    In a recent development, in March 2026, ABA representatives met with FATF evaluators at the Treasury Department’s request to explain recent efforts by the U.S. legal profession to combat money laundering. This included the ABA’s adoption and implementation of the 2023 amendments to Rule 1.16 of the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct concerning lawyers’ due diligence obligations.

    Recent findings suggest that the ABA is also urging Congress to promptly enact the Effective Assistance of Counsel in the Digital Era Act, which would protect the attorney-client privileged status of email communications between federally incarcerated people and their lawyers. Although U.S. mail, phone calls and in-person visits between lawyers and their incarcerated clients are shielded by attorney-client privilege, emails—the only rapid means for clients to reach their lawyers—are not. This is because the Federal Bureau of Prisons requires incarcerated people to waive the privilege in order to access the only available digital network.

    Industry observers note that the EACDEA would protect the confidentiality of incarcerated people’s email communications and, thus, their Sixth Amendment right to the effective assistance of counsel by ending the BOP’s mandated waiver of the privilege. The bill would require the government to obtain a warrant before accessing incarcerated people’s emails with their lawyers.

    According to recent reports, support for the bill’s passage, which has bipartisan co-sponsors in the House and Senate, has been a featured issue at the annual ABA Day in Washington, D.C., fly-in event three times. The ABA continues to lobby for its passage. At the same time, the ABA is seeking a voluntary change to the BOP’s practice by working with the bill’s champions to include report language in the fiscal year 2027 appropriations process reflecting congressional disapproval of the BOP’s waiver requirement.

    Industry observers note that as Congress and federal agencies continue to adopt or consider policies requiring disclosure of information protected by the attorney-client privilege or the lawyer’s duty of confidentiality, the ABA will remain vigilant in monitoring and opposing such measures. The association will also take all other steps necessary to safeguard the confidentiality protections essential to the effective assistance of counsel and the fair administration of justice.

    This report is written by the ABA Governmental Affairs Office and discusses advocacy efforts by the ABA relating to complications being addressed by Congress and the executive branch of the U.S. government. Follow @ABAGrassroots on social media.

    Supreme Court defers decision on whether to dismiss major gun case

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (480 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.
    • The skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case.
    • According to recent reports, lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order, which came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case, indicated that the justices would instead “defer[]” that ruling “pending oral argument,” which is scheduled for Wednesday, December 2.

    The skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case. Viramontes, who has been part of the challenge since it was filed in 2021, did not provide any explanation for his request.

    According to recent reports, lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue. They emphasized that Viramontes was a Cook County resident who said that he wanted to own an AR-15-style semiautomatic rifle. By contrast, they wrote, the other individual challenger in the case, Christopher Khaya, has said that he wants to own “an IMI Galil semiautomatic rifle,” which, according to Cook County, is not the kind of AR-15-style rifle covered by the question before the court.

    In a recent development, the challengers countered that the question presented is not limited to AR-15 rifles but also extends to “similar” semiautomatic rifles, which would include AK-47-style rifles like the IMI Galil. But in any event, they added, Khaya “also desires to possess an AR-15 platform rifle and would acquire one if it were lawful for him to do so.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in its order deferring a decision on whether the Cook County case is moot because of the dismissal of Viramontes from the case, the Supreme Court cited its 2023 decision in Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, in which it unanimously agreed after oral argument that the case was moot because the plaintiff had voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit in the lower court. But the chances that the court will ultimately reach the merits of the ban are likely higher than in Acheson, in which there was only one plaintiff, because the dispute over semiautomatic rifles encompasses not only multiple plaintiffs but also another case – a challenge to Connecticut’s ban on AR-15-style rifles.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    • Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers say the global water cycle has entered an âepoch of profound disruption.â.
    • (CN) â Global river flows and the amount of water held in lakes and reservoirs declined sharply during two years of exceptional heat, with freshwater resources falling to unprecedented levels in 2023 and 2024, researchers say in a new study published Thursday in Science.
    • Industry observers note that river discharge worldwide dropped 5.7% during the period, while active water storage in lakes and reservoirs fell 9.5% compared with the 1991-2020 average.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Chinese Academy of Sciences researchers say the global water cycle has entered an âepoch of profound disruption.â.

    (CN) â Global river flows and the amount of water held in lakes and reservoirs declined sharply during two years of exceptional heat, with freshwater resources falling to unprecedented levels in 2023 and 2024, researchers say in a new study published Thursday in Science.

    Industry observers note that river discharge worldwide dropped 5.7% during the period, while active water storage in lakes and reservoirs fell 9.5% compared with the 1991-2020 average. The losses were particularly severe in South America, where river flows fell nearly 18%, even as some areas experienced heavy rainfall and flooding.

    Led by Yongqiang Zhang, researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences examined global freshwater trends from 1991 through 2025, combining measurements from 150 major river basins with satellite observations of more than 1.2 million waterbodies.

    Their analysis found that river flows and surface water storage fluctuated considerably between 1991 and 2006 before remaining relatively stable through 2022. Both measures then declined sharply in 2023 and 2024. River flows showed signs of rebounding in 2025, but the researchers remarked the decline during the preceding two years was unprecedented in the historical record they examined.

    South America was particularly hard hit. Streamflow fell 17.8%, while water held in lakes and reservoirs decreased 16.5%.

    âThe global water cycle has already entered an Anthropocene epoch of profound disruption,â the researchers write.

    The researchers linked the losses to the combined effects of two ocean climate patterns. El NiÃ±o, which develops in the Pacific Ocean, generally reduces rainfall across the Amazon. During the same period, unusually warm conditions in the tropical North Atlantic further disrupted the movement of moisture toward northern South America.

    That combination intensified the region’s water shortages, even as other areas received enough rain to produce flooding.

    According to recent reports, the findings show extreme heat can coincide with declining freshwater resources even in regions that typically receive abundant rainfall. Scientists have generally expected climate change to bring heavier precipitation to wet areas and increased evaporation in dry ones, but declining river flows and depleted soil moisture point to more complicated changes.

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers!
    • In a recent development, following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30.
    • On Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers! We are very grateful for your support of our work. If you’d like to learn more about what the Supreme Court has noted about Thanksgiving, you can revisit our Closer Look on the topic from this time last year.

    In a recent development, following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30. The justices will hear eight total oral arguments during this session, addressing such concerns as the Second Amendment, deportations to “third-party countries,” and the seizure of an airplane over the illegal transportation of beer.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v. Cook County, on whether the Second Amendment guarantees a right to possess AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, but it did not take action on Cook County’s request to dismiss the case as moot. On Tuesday, the court confirmed that it had deferred action on that request until after oral argument, which will take place on Wednesday, December 2. The case name is now Khaya v. Cook County. For more on Tuesday’s announcement, see the On Site section below.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed tomorrow and Friday for Thanksgiving.

    Recent findings suggest that the December argument session will begin on Monday. That day, the justices will hear oral arguments in two cases: Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, on whether Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding, allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination; and Wassily v. Blanche, on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    On Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in Jouppi v. Alaska, an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane over the transport of beer into a dry village.

    On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Khaya v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, at 10:00 a.m. EST. As noted above, we will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    Jack Birle, Washington Examiner.

    In June 2022, the Supreme Court ruled “in Carson v. Makin that Maine could not exclude religious schools from a state program that allows parents to use vouchers for public or private schools for their children.” Now, a group of Catholic schools has asked the justices to revisit the program and address rules that were passed while the earlier case was pending “to bar schools from participating ... if their admissions policies prefer students of a certain religion, allow religious discrimination in their schools, or do not follow the state’s views on gender ideology,” according to the Washington Examiner. “The Catholic schools urge the Supreme Court to address multiple questions if it takes up the case, including whether to overrule the 1990 Supreme Court ruling Employment Division v. Smith, which found that the free exercise clause does not allow for people to violate a law as part of their religious practice, as long as the law is valid and neutral in how it is applied. The petition ... argues that Smith has allowed Maine to continue to exclude religious schools from state programs.”.

    Recent findings suggest that attorneys for Emily Bickford, a Maine mother “who has been prohibited from taking her 13-year-old daughter to church” in a custody order, appealed her challenge to the order to the Supreme Court last week. The order allows the child’s father “to solely decide on his daughter’s involvement with Calvary Chapel Church.” Bickford asks the justices to find that it violates “parental rights and religious liberty protections,” according to WMTW in Portland, Maine. “A parent’s ability to take her child to church during her own parenting time now depends on the State in which she lives,” Bickford’s petition for review says. “When a state court strips a fit parent of her right to direct her child’s religious upbringing and vests a co-parent with veto power, it deploys the coercive authority of the State to extinguish a fundamental right.”.

    Kanishka Singh and Julia Harte, Reuters.

    In a recent development, on Tuesday, “Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him a symbol for critics of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, left the US for Spain,” according to Reuters. His voluntarily departure brought an end to “a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court.” It began when “US authorities sent Abrego Garcia, who entered the US illegally, to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a prior court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.” For months, officials “mentioned they could not bring him back,” but the Supreme Court ultimately “ordered the government [to] facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return.” After he returned to the United States in June 2025, Abrego Garcia faced human smuggling charges “stemming from an earlier incident” and a renewed deportation effort.

    Gavin Bade, The Wall Street Journal.

    According to recent reports, since February, when the Supreme Court held that President Donald Trump did not have the authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose tariffs, the Trump administration has been using other statutes to rebuild the president’s tariff regime. This week, that effort will continue when the administration confirms increased “tariffs on China and dozens of other countries,” according to The Wall Street Journal. “The new tariffs will likely be added to levies from a separate tariff action, unveiled in July, that sought to penalize nations for not blocking the trade of goods produced with forced labor,” and target countries that the Trump administration has concluded are harming U.S. producers by “flood[ing] global markets with cheaper goods.” That July action sparked a new lawsuit over the administration’s tariff policies.

    On Monday, a panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit sided with President Donald Trump “in his fight to overturn his hush money criminal conviction in Latest York, ruling that a judge wrongly denied his effort to move the case into federal court,” according to The Hill. Trump’s current push to transfer the case “cites the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling.” The president contends that “he has the legal right to bring it up before a federal judge as a defense,” and the 2nd Circuit panel held on Monday that the district court did not properly consider this argument. “Monday’s decision effectively puts a halt to Trump’s ongoing appeal in New York’s state court system and moves it to federal court, where the president will continue pressing his arguments that the case should remain there.”.

    Philip Jankowski, The Dallas Morning News.

    According to recent reports, texas’ Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson said he will not defend the state’s “Ten Commandments classroom law,” just weeks before the justices are expected to consider whether to take up a challenge to it, according to The Dallas Morning News. “My jurisprudential opinion is that the law is unconstitutional,” Johnson said. “The court will have the ultimate say as to what’s constitutional and what is not, but I’m the one who states what the state’s position is, and it will not be the position the state has previously taken.” Outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton “cited Johnson’s unwillingness to defend the law as a reason the justices should decline to hear” the challenge to it in the state’s brief in opposition, which was filed on November 10. “If the Supreme Court stays out of the fight, a federal appeals court ruling upholding the classroom displays in Texas would remain in place, preserving a legal victory for Paxton even after he leaves office in January.”.

    With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case.

    It has been revealed that on Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the Closer Look section of this newsletter to covering the plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases. In this article, Blake took a step back and reflected on what we have learned.

    In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman analyzed each justice’s voting pattern in interim docket cases involving federal executive action, highlighting “a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.”.

    It has been revealed that in his Court Beyond Borders column, Martin Flaherty focused on the Supreme Court’s grant of review in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border. The case, according to Flaherty, will put “the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law” in the spotlight.

    Recent findings suggest that in her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1978’s Federal Communications Commission v. Pacifica Foundation, holding that the government may “constitutionally prohibit indecency even” when it falls “short of legal obscenity.” In a dissenting opinion, Justice William Brennan criticized the majority for “attempt[ing] to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people.”.

    In a recent development, (SCOTUSblog Plus) Since joining in 2022, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has forged a unique role on the Supreme Court. It often appears, as Amy noted in this analysis, that Jackson’s goal in dissenting opinions is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision of the law and speak to the public directly – regardless of whether anyone else on the court agrees.

    In his SCOTUSCrim column on Friday, Rory Little aimed “to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law” and explore “why that can be so interesting.”.

    Sarah Isgur and David French critique Congress’ current governing processes with the help of Michael “Frags” Fragoso, a partner at Torridon Law, and Nicholas Bagley, a professor of law at the University of Michigan and author of the book Why We Can’t Have Nice Things: How Legal Reformers Accidentally Broke America.

    The Closer Look in Wednesday editions is typically an entry in our Ask Amy series, in which Amy Howe answers reader questions about the Supreme Court.

    Q: At least for those of us of a certain age, the November 9 order list contained a familiar name in the “Attorney Discipline” section: Larry Klayman, perhaps best known as a frequent and fervent foe of the Clinton administration, had been “disbarred from the practice of law” in the Supreme Court. Which leads to the question: How, exactly, does someone get disbarred from the Supreme Court bar – especially if, like Klayman, they’ve never argued there?

    A: The answer (like so many others) can be found in the Supreme Court’s rules, starting with the rule that outlines how someone becomes eligible to join the Supreme Court bar, which is necessary not only to argue before the justices but also to sign filings there: lawyers must have been (among other things) “admitted to practice” in another jurisdiction for at least three years, and they cannot have been subject to any disciplinary proceedings during that time.

    Because becoming a member of the Supreme Court bar requires a clean disciplinary record, it follows that disciplinary problems can get a lawyer kicked out of the Supreme Court bar – even if the underlying conduct had nothing to do with the court itself. Specifically, the court’s rules provide for the suspension of any lawyer who “has been disbarred or suspended from practice in any court of record, or has engaged in conduct unbecoming a member of the Bar of this Court.” The suspended lawyer then has the chance to try to persuade the court “why disciplinary action should not be taken,” after which the court may take “any appropriate disciplinary action,” which can include disbarment.

    Industry observers note that in Klayman’s case, he was apparently suspended by the bar associations in the District of Columbia and Florida for alleged ethical violations in connection with his efforts to represent rancher Cliven Bundy in a federal court in Nevada, leading to his disbarment from the Supreme Court earlier this month. Klayman told Law360 that he looks to seek reconsideration of the Supreme Court’s order.

    “It is like having a latest in-law at Thanksgiving dinner. Uncle Fred will put on a clean shirt.”.

    — Chief Justice John Roberts’ thoughts when a new member joins the Supreme Court.

    • The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the Supreme Court on Monday will hear oral argument in Wassily v. Blanche, a case on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    Sources indicate that although the case will almost certainly be overshadowed by many of this term’s other immigration disputes – including Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on the Trump administration’s suspension of access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border – it may hold considerable consequences for noncitizens and bring new significance to the Trump administration’s effort to scale back asylum.

    The challengers in Wassily are two men who lost their asylum protections after being convicted of what immigration officials determined to be “particularly serious crime[s].”.

    It has been revealed that tamer Wassily was granted asylum in 2000 after raising concerns about facing religious persecution in his home country of Egypt. The Department of Homeland Security moved to terminate Wassily’s asylum protections after he was convicted in 2004 of third-degree stalking and child endangerment, beginning the process of deporting him back to Egypt.

    Byron Velasquez Arreaga came to the United States from Guatemala in 1995 and was granted asylum the following year. After Velasquez Arreaga was convicted of driving while intoxicated in 2015 and for aggravated driving while intoxicated in 2018, DHS indicated that it would terminate his asylum protections and move to deport him.

    It has been revealed that amid their removal proceedings, and after their asylum protections had been terminated, both Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga applied to become lawful permanent residents. This option is available to asylum recipients who meet certain requirements, including remaining in the United States for at least a year after receiving asylum protections, under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).

    In a recent development, after many years of complicated legal wrangling before immigration judges and the Board of Immigration Appeals, the men’s cases were considered together by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. The question before that court – and the question that is now before the Supreme Court – was whether noncitizens like Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga remain eligible for adjustment of immigration status under Section 1159(b) after their asylum protections have been terminated, because the statute refers to “any alien granted asylum” but is silent as to whether applicants must currently be asylees.

    In a 2-1 ruling, a 2nd Circuit panel rejected the men’s contention that “granted asylum” addresses a past decision – in which case anyone who had ever received asylum would be eligible for status adjustment under Section 11159(b) – and concluded that noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated are “categorically barr[ed]” from applying for adjustment to permanent legal status.

    Writing for the majority, Judge Richard Wesley emphasized the use of the word “status” in the opening of Section 1159(b), which reads: “The Secretary of Homeland Security or the Attorney General ... may adjust to the status of an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence the status of any alien granted asylum.” According to Wesley, a “natural reading of ‘the status of any alien granted asylum’ is that a noncitizen must presently be granted asylum to adjust to lawful permanent resident status under 8 U.S.C. § 1159(b).”.

    Sources indicate that in January, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga asked the Supreme Court to review the 2nd Circuit’s ruling, highlighting a disagreement between the federal courts of appeals over whether the phrase “granted asylum” in Section 1159(b) “refer[s] to a completed, historical event” or “a continuing, present status.” Like the 2nd Circuit, they noted, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit has held that noncitizens who have lost their asylum protections “are categorically ineligible” “for adjustment to [lawful permanent resident] status under Section 1159(b).” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, on the other hand, has held that such immigrants remain “eligible for adjustment.”.

    In late June, the justices granted review.

    In their brief on the merits, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga contend that the 2nd Circuit’s decision is out of step with the “[t]ext, context, structure, history, and purpose” of Section 1159(b). In particular, they highlight several nearby passages in which lawmakers explicitly imposed “continuing conditions” that address a termination of immigration status, asserting that Congress “could have and would have” included such a condition here if it intended to unambiguously bar former asylees from applying for lawful permanent residency.

    The two men also point to Section 1159(c), which grants the DHS secretary and attorney general the authority to waive portions of the statute “for humanitarian purposes, to assure family unity, or when it is otherwise in the public interest.” Holding that adjustment to lawful permanent residency is categorically unavailable to noncitizens whose asylum protections have been terminated “would take core parts of that discretion away,” the men write. Such a limitation cuts against Congress’ purpose for allowing for discretion, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga argue. “There are many reasons why Congress would want” these officials “to retain discretion” here, they say, including that termination sometimes stems from factors “entirely outside” an asylee’s control. For example, the immigration status of the spouse and children of an asylee is often linked to the asylee’s status. If the noncitizen who was originally granted asylum loses his or her status, so does the whole family.

    Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga ask the justices to recognize that, at the very least, the text of Section 1159(b) is unclear and to apply the rule of lenity, which they describe as a “well-settled and longstanding principle” under which “ambiguous provisions leading to the severe sanction of removal should be construed in favor of the noncitizen.” The Supreme Court “has repeatedly restated and reaffirmed that rule,” they conclude.

    In its merits brief, the federal government counters that Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s interpretation of Section 1159(b) defies common sense. The text of the statute, according to U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, describes a “transition from one status (that of an ‘alien granted asylum’) to another (that of an ‘alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence’).” If an immigrant is no longer at that starting point because his asylum status has been terminated, he can’t make the transition, Sauer asserts.

    The government contends that the “statutory context” supports this interpretation, because, in nearby passages, “alien granted asylum” clearly refers to a noncitizen’s “present status.” For example, in Section 1158(c)(1), “Congress identified benefits available to an ‘alien granted asylum,’ including protection from removal and work authorization,” according to Sauer. “Those benefits undisputedly cease when asylum status is terminated.”.

    In a recent development, the government rejects the idea that barring noncitizens who have lost their asylum status from applying for a green card would interfere with the authority of the DHS secretary and attorney general to exercise discretion. Officials, Sauer writes, would remain free to intervene at an earlier point to prevent the termination of asylum status in the first place.

    In a recent development, sauer concludes by urging the justices to reject what he characterizes as a “last-resort appeal to lenity” – that is, Wassily and Velasquez Arreaga’s claim that Section 1159(b) is an “ambiguous provision[]” and should therefore be interpreted in their favor. He argues that the rule of lenity does not apply here, not just because the meaning of the provision is clear, but also because Section 1159(b) does not directly address deportation, which is the context in which the rule of lenity arises.

    The Supreme Court’s decision in Wassily v. Blanche is expected by early July at the latest.

    Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

    #227591. Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1881 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding.
    • According to recent reports, the plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system.
    • According to recent reports, machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding. On November 30, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in a dispute over whether the law allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination, or whether such employees must instead rely on a different federal law, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, that specifically provides a remedy for sex-based employment discrimination but also imposes constraints not found in Title IX. The employees seeking to bring the lawsuits under Title IX will face a bench that has become increasingly reluctant to permit private plaintiffs to bring lawsuits unless the federal statute at concern clearly authorizes them.

    According to recent reports, the plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system. Thomas Crowther worked as an art professor at Augusta University. When he was accused of inappropriate conduct by several students, including sexual harassment, the university initially suspended him for one semester and then declined to renew his contract, prompting Crowther to file a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

    According to recent reports, machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech. She was fired in 2019 after an investigation raised concerns about mistreatment of players. Before her termination, Joseph had repeatedly complained about her team receiving fewer resources than the men’s team. Joseph filed a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

    The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit considered Crowther’s and Joseph’s cases together. It held that Title IX does not provide a right – either explicitly or by implication – for employees to sue for sex discrimination. When the full court declined to reconsider their case, Crowther and Joseph asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, which it agreed in May to do.

    Sources indicate that crowther and Joseph urge the justices to reverse the 11th Circuit’s decision and allow their lawsuits to go forward. They point to the text of Title IX, which provides that “[n]o person … shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” That language, they say, creates a broad ban on sex discrimination by schools that receive federal funding; moreover, they add, Title IX “also contains ‘a list of narrow exceptions’ that does not include employment discrimination” – further evidence that Congress intended Title IX’s ban on sex discrimination to apply to both employees and students.

    The Georgia university system agrees that Title IX bars sex discrimination in employment, “and that federal agencies may deny funding to violators.” But that is not the question before the court, it stresses. Instead, it emphasizes, the issue is whether Title IX allows employees to bring private lawsuits alleging that they were the victims of sex-based discrimination. The answer, the university system states, is no.

    It has been revealed that to support their position, Crowther and Joseph cite several past Supreme Court rulings, including its 1982 decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell. In Bell, the court upheld regulations, meant to implement Title IX, that barred sex-based discrimination against employees (as well as students) at federally funded educational institutions. That decision, they say, demonstrates that Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination in employment. “The Court’s cases, read together,” they continue, “lead to the inexorable conclusion that an employee who is a victim of intentional sex-based discrimination by a federally funded education program or activity has a private right of action to seek damages under Title IX.”.

    According to recent reports, crowther and Joseph add that the Supreme Court has allowed employment discrimination lawsuits under other federal antidiscrimination statutes that apply to the recipients of federal funds – Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin, and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which prohibits discrimination based on disability. Those laws, they write, contain “virtually identical” language – further evidence that Title IX allows lawsuits like theirs.

    The university pushes back against the employees’ attempt to draw comparisons with other federal antidiscrimination laws. It writes that Supreme Court “has assumed,” but has never specifically held, that “Title VI permits private suits for the narrow category of employment discrimination that statute prohibits.” But in any event, it claims, that assumption does not indicate anything about whether Congress created a private remedy in Title IX. The university system also emphasizes that “[t]he Rehabilitation Act has always been a far more detailed and targeted statute than Title IX” – for example, it “expressly ban[s] disability discrimination by the federal government as [an] employer.”.

    Similarly, the university system continues, the Supreme Court’s decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell does not resolve the question before the justices now. The court in that case, it writes, “had no reason to, and did not, consider whether Congress created a private remedy atop the express one the challenged regulations implemented.”.

    Whether the availability of another remedy forecloses private lawsuits under Title IX.

    Sources indicate that the Supreme Court, the university system writes, has made clear that the right to bring a private lawsuit hinges on whether there is “evidence confirming that Congress sought to” provide such a right. And when Congress has created “an express remedy” in another statute, there is “a strong ‘presumption’ that Congress did not imply others” – particularly when that “express remedy” involves a “‘comprehensive’ remedial scheme.”.

    It has been revealed that that is exactly what happened here, the university system argues. “Mere weeks before Congress passed Title IX,” the university contends, “it extended … [the] protection—and reticulated enforcement scheme” in Title VII to school employees, which bars employment discrimination based on (among other things) sex. Therefore, the university system says, allowing lawsuits like Crowther’s and Joseph’s to go forward under Title IX “would attribute to the same Congress an inexplicable about-face: Immediately after giving a set of employees a private employment-discrimination remedy mediated by a ‘detailed administrative and judicial process,’ it silently gave the same employees a second private right of action, to attack the same basic harm.” And it did so, the university system suggests, without requiring employees to comply with any of the “strings attached” to private lawsuits under Title VII – including, but not limited to, the requirement to first file a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission before going to court and its limits on the damages that can be recovered.

    Crowther and Joseph counter that “Title IX and Title VII are ‘vastly different.’” The prospect “that an employee might be able to bring a claim under both Title IX and Title VII does not justify” a determination that a private right of action is not available under Title IX. Rather, they write, the Supreme Court “has recognized that Congress has enacted overlapping remedies to eradicate employment discrimination, and Congress chose not to exclude employment discrimination from Title IX’s broad reach.”.

    According to recent reports, as additional support for the idea that Title IX does not provide a private right of action for employees, the university system notes that the law was enacted pursuant to Congress’ power under the Constitution’s Spending Clause, which gives Congress the power to impose taxes and spend money for (among other things) the country’s “general welfare.” In exchange for the federal funds, the recipients therefore agree to comply with the conditions that Congress imposes, and Congress can terminate the funding if a recipient fails to do so. However, in cases such as last term’s Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety, the Supreme Court has held that additional sanctions for violating the conditions in a law, such as the ability to bring a private lawsuit, are only available if the recipient has knowingly and voluntarily agreed to those sanctions. Here, the university system asserts, “Title IX does not unambiguously authorize private employment-discrimination suits,” and so it could not have known that it could be sued by employees, much less have agreed to that possibility.

    Sources indicate that crowther and Joseph reject this argument. They say that recipients of Title IX funds “‘have been on notice that they could be subjected to private suits for intentional sex discrimination under Title IX since 1979.’” As a result, they write, the Supreme Court’s “Spending Clause precedents ‘do[] not preclude private suits for intentional acts that clearly violate Title IX.’”.

    A “friend of the court” brief from West Virginia and 20 other states attempts to refute this assertion. The states tell the justices that the states “are best positioned to say what Title IX’s bargain contains, as they’re the ones who’ve accepted it.” And they “can say with firsthand authority that the deal they made did not include this,” they write. “To the contrary, all the circumstances suggested to the States that Title VII [procedures, not private lawsuits] was the rightful home for those cases.”.

    The Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting the university system, urges the justices not to reach the Spending Clause question at all. Instead, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the justices, they “should decide this case on the ground that” the employees’ “claims fail as a matter of ‘statutory interpretation’ alone.” Therefore, he writes, it is “unnecessary to reach, and prudent to avoid, the parties’ further dispute over the constitutional notice requirement for legislation enacted under Congress’s spending power.”.

    The possible effects of the court’s decision.

    Industry observers note that both the Trump administration and lawyers representing public school districts warn that a ruling in the employees’ favor could have “significant adverse consequences.” The federal government suggests that allowing lawsuits like the employees’ to go forward “would crowd judicial dockets with premature lawsuits that could often be avoided through proper use of Title VII’s administrative process, which successfully resolves numerous cases. And it would undermine the government’s primary authority to enforce both Title VII … and Title IX.”.

    It has been revealed that for its part, the National School Attorneys Association emphasizes that “public school districts typically operate with limited legal and administrative staff. Expanding Title IX’s implied private right of action to cover claims against employees,” it says, “would impose disproportionate compliance and litigation burdens on public school districts and diminish the limited resources they have to educate students.”.

    It has been revealed that but a brief from the National Education Association, supporting the employees, takes a contrary stance. It tells the justices that upholding the 11th Circuit’s decision “would remove a critical deterrent against sex-based mistreatment of educators, exacerbate an already dire workforce crisis, and ultimately compromise the quality of education available to millions of students nationwide.” Lawsuits under Title VII, it writes, are not enough because that law “does not offer the full protections to which employees of education programs are entitled.”.

    A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #227588. Court to determine if Alaska’s seizure of pilot’s plane for carrying beer violates the Eighth Amendment

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1760 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Court to determine if Alaska’s seizure of pilot’s plane for carrying beer violates the Eighth Amendment

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane.
    • According to recent reports, the case before the court began in April 2012, when Jouppi, who is now 83 years old, was scheduled to fly a passenger from Fairbanks to Beaver, Alaska – less than a one-hour flight.
    • Before Jouppi took off for Beaver, state troopers arrived at the airport with a warrant to search his plane.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane. Prosecutors sought that forfeiture on the theory that the pilot, Ken Jouppi, must have known a passenger was bringing beer to an Alaskan village where alcohol is prohibited. That penalty, Jouppi argues, violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on excessive fines.

    According to recent reports, the case before the court began in April 2012, when Jouppi, who is now 83 years old, was scheduled to fly a passenger from Fairbanks to Beaver, Alaska – less than a one-hour flight. Beaver, whose population was reported as 48 in the 2020 census, is a “dry” village: it bars not only the sale of alcohol, but also the importation and possession of alcohol. There are no roads to or from the village, and the closest hospital is in Fairbanks.

    Before Jouppi took off for Beaver, state troopers arrived at the airport with a warrant to search his plane. According to the state, law enforcement officials had “receiv[ed] information that Jouppi had repeatedly transported passengers with alcohol to” dry villages. They found the equivalent of three cases of beer that his passenger was bringing to her husband, who works in Beaver, and charged both the passenger and Jouppi (as well as his firm) with knowingly bringing alcohol to a “dry” village.

    The passenger pleaded guilty. Jouppi went to trial, where he was found guilty. The trial judge sentenced him to three days in prison and ordered him to pay a fine of $1,500.

    Under state law, prosecutors also sought to forfeit Jouppi’s plane. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled that the forfeiture did not violate the Constitution. It concluded that “the forfeiture of Jouppi’s airplane is not grossly disproportional to the gravity of the offense for which he has been convicted and, therefore … does not violate the Excessive Fines Clause of the Eighth Amendment.”.

    Industry observers note that jouppi then came to the Supreme Court last year. He asked the justices to decide whether, to determine if a fine violates the Excessive Fines Clause, courts should consider the gravity of the specific defendant’s conduct. The court agreed in July to take up his case.

    Jouppi and Alaska disagree on virtually every aspect of the dispute – not only the legal issues and conclusions, but also the facts. Although he denied knowing that any beer was on the plane, Jouppi characterizes the case as one hinging on just one six-pack of beer – which, state troopers testified, was visible in a grocery bag.

    Sources indicate that jouppi urges the Supreme Court to reverse the Alaska Supreme Court’s decision and send the case back to the lower court for it to take another look, stressing that “[t]he Excessive Fines Clause was built for cases like this.” He points to the Supreme Court’s 1998 decision in United States v. Bajakajian, in which the justices agreed that requiring a defendant to forfeit $357,144 for violating a federal law that required him to report that he was taking more than $10,000 in cash out of the country was unconstitutional. “As the Court has recognized,” Jouppi contends, “a forfeiture … violates the Excessive Fines Clause if it is ‘grossly disproportional to the gravity of a defendant’s offense.’” Moreover, he continues, in making that determination, courts should look at “the gravity of a defendant’s offense … not purely in the abstract, but with reference to the defendant’s own wrongdoing” – both his own culpability and “‘the gravity of the actual offense giving rise to forfeiture.’”.

    However, Jouppi suggests, the Alaska Supreme Court instead “evaluated [his] wrongdoing at a stratospheric level of abstraction,” by looking broadly at the harm that the plane-forfeiture law was intended to address rather than any harm that Jouppi himself might have caused by flying a six-pack of Budweiser into Beaver. When a court looks at wrongdoing “purely in the abstract,” Jouppi tells the justices, “the societal harm of even the most minor infraction will dwarf any fine imaginable.” For example, he says, in 2019, the failure to wear a seatbelt led to more than 2,000 deaths and 46,000 serious injuries, at a cost of $11 billion; the costs of speeding-related accidents amounted to $46 billion. But it would be “grossly disproportional,” Jouppi asserts, for the government to require the forfeiture of a car whenever someone failed to wear a seatbelt or went one mile per hour over the speed limit.

    The Alaska Supreme Court was also wrong, Jouppi continues, when it concluded that the forfeiture of Jouppi’s $95,000 plane was not grossly disproportional because that value was “only” nine-and-a-half times the maximum fine that could be imposed under state law for any class A misdemeanor, which could also include (among other things) selling alcohol to a minor, “the unauthorized practice of law, medicine, or osteopathy,” indecent exposure to a child, domestic violence in a child’s presence, “misconduct involving a corpse,” and bestiality. “That a worst-case animal abuser, or corpse abuser, or faux-osteopath could merit a $10,000 fine sheds no light on ‘the gravity of [Jouppi’s] crime’ or whether forfeiting an airplane for a six-pack is excessive,” Jouppi emphasizes.

    In a recent development, alaska paints a very different picture, countering that “Jouppi’s crime was not flying in ‘a six-pack.’” Instead, it writes, “Jouppi loaded two cases of beer and four six-packs of 16-ounce beers on his plane destined for a village of a mere 48 people with no roads in or out and no emergency medical services.” It explains that the law allowing villages like Beaver to prohibit alcohol are a response to “the destruction caused by alcohol in its isolated, rural communities.” And because alcohol “often arrives by plane” in remote villages, state law requires a pilot who is convicted of knowingly transporting alcohol into a dry community to forfeit his plane. That penalty, the state notes, both “prevents the airplane from being used again to import alcohol and deters others from doing the same.”.

    The state contends that “Jouppi fights a strawman” by “insisting that the Alaska Supreme Court considered his offense ‘purely in the abstract’”; rather, that court upheld “the forfeiture of Jouppi’s airplane … as applied to Jouppi’s actual circumstances.” In doing so, Alaska indicates, it “reviewed and considered all the facts that led up to Jouppi’s conviction for knowingly transporting alcohol into a dry village. Jouppi’s actions fell squarely within the conduct targeted by the law, and he threatened to cause the same harm feared by the legislature. Whether Jouppi knew about all or just some of the nine gallons of beer he loaded onto his plane does not change the constitutional analysis.”.

    Moreover, the state continues, “Alaska’s forfeiture regime is not unusual or extreme.” The state points to a long history of federal laws requiring “the forfeiture of ships used to commit a host of crimes, including customs fraud, piracy, and the slave trade.” And indeed, it notes, when Alaska became a territory, “Congress imposed similar punishments” there, requiring ships to be forfeited “for the illegal killing of fur-bearing animals and the importation of alcohol. Those laws, like Alaska’s now, deterred hard-to-detect crimes and incapacitated criminals from using the vessel to repeat the offense.”.

    Finally, the state distinguishes the history of laws requiring the forfeiture of ships and planes from those involving “forfeitures of currency, such as that in Bajakajian.” Like the provision of English law on which it was based, the Excessive Fines Clause, it writes, was intended to serve as “a rebuke of ‘huge monetary penalties’ assessed by the King’s judges against his enemies.” Courts assess those penalties, the state argues, by looking at the “‘value of the fine in relation to the offense.’” But when considering “punitive forfeitures of vessels and other instrumentalities of crime,” the state stresses, the inquiry focuses on “whether the forfeiture is limited to the property ‘“tainted” by unlawful use’” – precisely the situation in Jouppi’s case.

    Like Jouppi and the state, the “friends of the court” briefs filed supporting each side take very different positions.

    A brief supporting Jouppi from the group Fair and Just Prosecution contends that “[f]ines and forfeitures in this country have evolved beyond their intended purpose of retribution and deterrence” and “now function as a revenue-generating tool that can fill budget gaps without formally raising taxes.” “Mandatory forfeiture statutes” like the one at matter in this case, the group argues, “create not only disproportionate punishments, like Jouppi’s, but also the perception that the system has self-serving goals other than public safety in mind.”.

    Another brief supporting Jouppi, from the Pacific Legal Foundation, pushes back against the idea that a court should consider the constitutionality of the forfeiture of Jouppi’s plane in light of the harm that the forfeiture law was intended to address. “The Court should analyze the confiscation of a person’s property based on individual culpability,” the group argues, “because the Constitution protects individual rights.”.

    By contrast, a “friend of the court” brief from the Alaska Legislative Council, a bipartisan committee formed to (among other things) represent the state’s legislature when it is not in session, stresses that the legislature enacted the plane-forfeiture law as “a calibrated response to a crisis unparalleled elsewhere,” “recogniz[ing] that the extraordinary isolation of rural Alaska villages, coupled with the complete dearth of public-safety infrastructure in many such communities, left residents uniquely vulnerable.” The Supreme Court, the council states, “has made clear that ‘judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature.’”.

    Industry observers note that former U.S. Attorney General William Barr, along with three former Alaska attorneys general, also filed a brief supporting the state. They argue that “Jouppi’s proposed rule would” in fact “reach far beyond Beaver” to other “Alaska Native” communities, where it would “systematically understate the gravity of offenses in the communities where deterrence and prevention matter most.” Barr and the other lawyers tell the court that “[t]he question in this case is not whether six beers, standing alone, could cause every alcohol-related harm in rural Alaska. The question is whether the Constitution requires a court to pretend that Jouppi’s six beers were headed nowhere in particular, threatened nothing, and could have been conveyed by some other means. It does not.”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    • Consumer behavior is changing, and marketers hunting for incremental growth need to look beyond traditional discovery.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Snap’s Head of Performance Marketing GTM Rick Lucas and Kitsch CMO Ying Ying Kuang on why relying on last-click attribution hides your best customers, and how Clicks + Deterministic Views (CDV) paint a fuller picture of conversion.

    Consumer behavior is changing, and marketers hunting for incremental growth need to look beyond traditional discovery.

    As audiences turn to DMs and group chats to make purchase decisions, standard last-click platform reports miss authentic peer recommendations.

    In this episode of Inside the Stack, Snap’s Head of Performance Marketing GTM, Rick Lucas, and Kitsch CMO Ying Ying Kuang explain why last-click attribution—while still essential—isn’t the whole story.

    They discuss how Kitsch used a 16% geo-lift holdout test to prove Snap’s incremental value beyond the click, why Clicks + Deterministic Views (CDV) are necessary to capture real demand, and how to get comfortable living in the “messy middle” of continuous testing.

    #227581. Oh yeah, GTA VI is the good stuff for streamers

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (752 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    Oh yeah, GTA VI is the good stuff for streamers

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, asmongold & co.
    • Recent findings suggest that the long-long-awaited Rockstar title that’s turning out to be “a bug zapper for chuds” is officially the single biggest video game ever made.
    • Of course, all this hype has translated into enormous traffic for digital video platforms and the creators who stock them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, asmongold & co. might be major mad that Grand Theft Auto VI‘s story hinges on being good to your über-hot girlfriend, but everyone else is diggin’ it.

    Recent findings suggest that the long-long-awaited Rockstar title that’s turning out to be “a bug zapper for chuds” is officially the single biggest video game ever made. It cleared $3.8 billion in sales on day one, and has the second-highest critics’ consensus rating of all time, outdone only by Nintendo‘s 1998 masterpiece The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (which just got a nice remake that released nearly in tandem with GTA VI).

    Of course, all this hype has translated into enormous traffic for digital video platforms and the creators who stock them.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Twitch also saw a 33% bump in the number of channels going live: It peaked at almost ~200,000 concurrent live channels, with GTA VI making up 127,400 of them.

    YouTube Gaming, meanwhile, drew 33.2 million watch hours, and Kick generated 48.4 million.

    Now, to be clear, these are not GTA VI-specific numbers. These are across entire platforms. But it’s a good look at things holistically, because as GTA VI rose, other titles’ traffic seeped toward it.

    Recent findings suggest that on Twitch, GTA VI streams generated 76.81 million watch hours in the first 48 after its release. And though it didn’t include numbers, Streams Charts reports that “[h]undreds of creators also set personal audience records as fans tuned in to watch their first steps in Rockstar’s latest release.”.

    Nearly every other top title fell in watch hours, including World of Warcraft (down 31%), League of Legends (down 7%), Dota 2 (down 12%), Counter-Strike (31%), and Fortnite (39%).

    The only game that didn’t lose traction was Escape from Tarkov, which went up 11%; this is due to developer Battlestate Games holding a Twitch Drops giveaway during this timeframe, where streamers are required to broadcast Tarkov gameplay, and viewers are incentivized to tune in because they’ll get exclusive in-game items.

    The game that saw one of the biggest traffic drops was, perhaps unsurprisingly, Grand Theft Auto V, whose viewership plummeted 49%. (More on that in a minute.).

    Over on Kick, Streams Charts spotted an interesting data point: While Just Chatting streams had a 19% drop on Twitch during the first 48 hours, Kick’s Just Sleeping category jumped 176% thanks to streamers holding 24/7 GTA VI marathon streams where they left things running while they caught catnaps.

    Things got muddy on YouTube. Streams Charts reports that many streamers went live under the GTA V category instead of GTA VI, “making it virtually impossible to separate interest in the older game from traffic driven by the upcoming release.”.

    It has been revealed that streams Charts tracked YouTube watch time falls in top games like Fortnite (60%) and Mobile Legends: Bang Bang (30.4%), while Apex Legends and Free Fire rose 70% and 59%, respectively. Like with Tarkov‘s Twitch traffic, Apex and Free Fire‘s boosts were thanks to view-generating events. In Apex‘s case, it was invitational tournament FFL APEX BLOCK PARTY, and for Free Fire, it was the FFWS Global Finals 2026 competition.

    In two days, GTA VI‘s total watch hours (counted across Twitch, YouTube, Kick, and eight other platforms) beat all other game debuts’ first-week numbers.

    The closest to catching it is Valorant, which dropped in April 2020 and generated 150.48 million watch hours in its first seven days. Then there’s Elden Ring, which dropped February 2022 to 79.08M hours, and Diablo IV in June 2023 to 74.34M hours. Hogwarts Legacy, Cyberpunk 2077, and Resident Evil Requiem are all down in the 40-60M hours range.

    Sources indicate that now, this does not mean any game will lose traffic long-term, aside from potentially GTA V. Here’s why: GTA VI is the shiny fresh thing on the block. Once streamers churn through its story, most will go back to their usual niches. The ones who stick around post-campaign will be playing GTA VI Online, and those are the folks that were probably still streaming GTA V when VI came out.

    Sources indicate that GTA has one of the biggest roleplaying communities of any game, and VI provides an expansive new playground for folks who are into that. Everyone else will enjoy the campaign and the viewership bump it brings, then head back to Apex or WoW or League of Legends.

    Why Mobile Apps Treasure Downtime; Terms Of Non-Endearment

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.
    • Industry observers note that but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for consumers’ downtime?
    • It has been revealed that people using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    Industry observers note that but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for consumers’ downtime? That’s the case made by Felix Braberg, a mobile ad and monetization consultant, in a blog post.

    It has been revealed that people using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it. Meanwhile, both DoorDash and Uber have billion-dollar annual ad businesses, but they’re not rushing to build their own gaming or streaming offerings. So they’re natural fits for app advertisers looking to help users pass the time.

    In a recent development, appLovin’s strength in mobile gaming is not so dissimilar. But AppLovin has a nascent consumer advertising segment now, and a few of its early advertisers have noted the power of reaching people while they’re playing games on the toilet. It doesn’t get more “downtime” than that.

    Gaming can fit neatly into the downtime vacuum that right now is awkwardly filled by ads or nothing. But successfully advertising a mobile game traditionally required a user to download the game and leave the app where they saw it advertised.

    Now, though, startups such as PlaysOut are integrating mobile games directly into other apps and monetizing those experiences with rewarded video. It’s a way for nongaming apps to capitalize on the downtime that benefits gaming.

    Which leads Braberg to predict that the next wave of mobile growth “will come from apps that were never game companies.”.

    Scarcely a week after launching ChatGPT’s new Business Hub, designed to let businesses see how they’re performing in ChatGPT, OpenAI has revised the Hub’s terms of service, Digiday reports.

    The revisions came soon after Digiday reached out to OpenAI, citing legal concerns brought forward by lawyers on behalf of publishers.

    Some of those legal restrictions have been removed in the revised terms of service. However, the revised terms also introduced more restrictions, such as requiring companies to waive their right to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data.

    But, while OpenAI is still imposing some legal restrictions on companies that use its Business Hub, “they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse,” an IP and tech lawyer who requested anonymity tells Digiday. “A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages.”.

    The Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons has been amassing a collection of consumer- and business-facing software vendors that kind of resembles the Island of Misfit Toys. It added another dud (or stud?) to its stable last week.

    Bending Spoons will acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for about $3.7 billion, less than a third of what Intuit paid a decade ago, Reuters reports.

    In a recent development, bending Spoons also recently added the online whiteboard Miro and location-based pet-tracking service Tractive, plus once-promising internet companies Brightcove, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo and AOL. Its business model is akin to private equity, in that it acquires struggling companies and drastically reduces headcount while raising prices or removing free tiers. Interestingly, advertising is an ancillary part of its model.

    To be clear, AOL and Vimeo haven’t quit on ad revenue. But Bending Spoons is focused on subscription revenue growth and consolidated cost savings, rather than building an identity spine for advertising and data sales.

    Recent findings suggest that but Bending Spoons still must demonstrate that it can turn flatlined businesses (Mailchimp declined year over year, for instance) into earners. Which is a bit like trying to bend a spoon using only your mind.

    Great news on the turnaround front: Bending Spoons reported 125% revenue growth last week.

    In a recent development, but there’s some not-so-great news, too: Its organic growth was an anemic 3%. So growth is coming from net-newly introduced businesses, with these acquisitions contributing some $4 billion in debt.

    In a recent development, apple is developing its own autonomous AI agents. [Bloomberg].

    Industry observers note that will Anthropic eventually launch an ads business? [Digiday].

    It has been revealed that the Nasdaq enters its third correction of 2026 amid a painful tech investor slide. [NYT].
