    #227576. The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1030 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wall Street loves to pile on ad tech.
    • No manufacturer has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.
    • TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the company selling the media sitting in the room.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wall Street loves to pile on ad tech. They’re all about you when you’re up and quick to dismiss you when you’re down.

    No manufacturer has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.

    TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the company selling the media sitting in the room. That idea remains true, and it is the reason TTD became the largest independent DSP in the world.

    So what changed? TTD latched onto a new principle: the defense of the open internet. Which means the company built its core value prop around a shrinking portion of where consumers spend their time and where advertisers spend their money.

    As DV360 became Google’s Death Star, The Trade Desk was the Rebel Alliance standing up for the open web. But while TTD spent the last several years proving they were the anti-Google, Amazon snuck in the back door and changed the whole DSP market.

    It has been revealed that if The Trade Desk holds to its first principle and lets go of the second, its value becomes more obvious than ever. Three moves would signal a new era for the manufacturer:.

    1. Separate the value prop of “open internet” with objective decisioning. The firm should retire the open internet as its stated purpose and replace it with what all advertisers value: independent, data-driven decisioning for brands and agencies. The open web stays in the portfolio as one channel among several, allowing buyers to see the whole field.

    Sources indicate that 2. Offer an objective view of the walled gardens. Google will not let a third-party DSP bid on YouTube, and Meta has shown no interest in opening its auction. But neither fact prevents The Trade Desk from ingesting platform reporting, independent measurement and content data from nearly every walled garden, then normalizing it against its own CTV and open web buys.

    3. Save the open internet by showing the whole picture. TTD taking an objective view of all platforms would highlight measurement and quality discrepancies. Which would, in turn, improve the open internet’s reputation in the eyes of the buy side. Without that full view, there is no way to show how “premium” open internet performs against the largest user-generated platforms in the world.

    From the beginning, The Trade Desk owned no inventory at all. It had no financial reason to steer a dollar anywhere except where the data said it would work for the buyer.

    TTD’s 2016 S-1 organized the firm’s strengths under headings like “We Do Not Arbitrage Advertising Inventory” and “We Are Data-Driven.” The phrase “open internet” does not appear in the company’s prospectus summary or risk factors at all.

    The business built on that positioning worked extremely well. TTD went public in September 2016, grew revenue from $308 million in 2017 to $2.44 billion in 2024, reached a market cap of roughly $40 billion by 2021 and met or beat expectations for 33 consecutive quarters.

    Industry observers note that in 2025, growth slowed and stock performance followed suit. That slowing growth is the natural effect of being the Pied Piper of the shrinking “open web.”.

    It has been revealed that redseer Strategy Consultants estimate that the programmatic open web gets only 20%-30% of ad budgets, with 70%-80% of programmatic spend going to walled gardens. This split has held for roughly five years.

    Advertisers have already made their decision. Budgets did not follow time spent, because walled gardens offer simplicity that programmatic cannot: an easy button for efficient reach. While the value of that reach can be debated, the easy way won.

    The concentration of spend is still increasing. EMarketer expects Google, Meta and Amazon to take 62.3% of worldwide digital ad spend in 2026, with Meta at about $243 billion and Google at about $240 billion. Amazon is forecast to grow from $69 billion in 2025 to $97 billion in 2027. Every incremental dollar in those forecasts is a dollar that an independent DSP cannot bid on today. Forecasts are growing faster than the open web.

    It has been revealed that television was supposed to be the market where the “open internet” reclaimed ground with upper-funnel brands. Except CTV is also becoming a walled garden medium. In Nielsen’s May 2026 Gauge, YouTube accounted for 13.8% of all US TV viewing, making Google the single largest media distributor in the US.

    Advertisers have limited transparency into the AI products of each walled garden. The content itself is UGC (and increasingly AI-generated). The measurement is dictated by the platform. And yet marketers need to spend there in order to get reach and efficiency. Imagine if there were a truly objective way to spend those dollars?

    None of this means that TTD’s founding principle failed. It means the principle is aimed at an open web target that keeps getting smaller. An objective buyer that can only see 20%-30% of the budget is no longer willing to spend the time, money and energy on the shrinking pie.

    CMOs have one budget. The question they actually want answered is where the next dollar should go across YouTube, Meta, TikTok, Snap, CTV and the web, backed by objective data. Today, nobody independently answers that question. The Trade Desk is the only firm in the industry that is poised to provide a solution.

    In a recent development, most turnarounds require a firm to find a upcoming reason to exist, and most of them fail because the new reason is never as convincing as the original one. This turnaround just requires The Trade Desk to remember its original reason for being.

    When The Trade Desk opens up its view beyond the open web, Wall Street – and the buy side – will rejoice.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Back in March, Facebook doubled down on its efforts to woo creators from other platforms by launching Creator Fast Track—a program that pays established creators up to $3,000 a month (for a max of three months) to start posting Reels on Facebook.

    Industry observers note that now, the Meta-owned platform is expanding that initiative to include U.S. college students with as few as 1,000 followers on Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube. Among other perks, Creator Fast Track College Edition offers eligible creators “immediate access to Facebook Content Monetization” and “increased reach on eligible reels” (per Meta).

    College students with larger followings can also access bonuses that provide “three months of guaranteed pay for sharing eligible reels.” According to Meta, “Creators with at least 20,000 followers on Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube can earn between $100-$450 per month, those with at least 100,000 followers can earn $1,000 per month, and those with more than one million followers can earn $3,000 per month.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    It has been revealed that facebook’s creator payouts hit an all-time high last year at almost $3 billion—a 35% increase from 2024 (per Meta). Reels accounted for 60% of that total, while the rest went to Stories, photos, and text posts.

    That growing investment in creators—especially short-form video creators—is clear evidence of Facebook’s determination to compete more directly with rivals like TikTok and YouTube.

    And it’s not just targeting big-name creators, either; as Creator Fast Track’s lower entry point for college students highlights, Facebook is eager to attract young creators at the start of their careers.

    Industry observers note that the rising importance of NIL rights and trends like #RushTok and #DormTok makes that a smart move. Since 2021, student athletes have carved out a bigger and bigger space for themselves in the creator economy, attracting the attention of major brands and platforms.

    Content creation has also become a strong Proposal B for NIL athletes who may not go pro after college. If Facebook can become a key platform for those creators while they’re still in school, it has a better shot at keeping them around after graduation—whether they go pro or pivot to full-time content creation.

    #227573. AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (687 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    AI Needs To Cite Its Sources. This Consumer Intelligence Platform Ensures It Does

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Stravito was debuted roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.
    • Now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution.
    • At the crux of the company is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Stravito was debuted roughly nine years ago, its goal was to help brands put the right product in front of the right consumer early in their shopping journey.

    Now, in the age of generative AI, its focus hasn’t changed so much as its structure and execution. Stravito, which touts itself as a consumer intelligence platform, uses AI to help marketers better understand their customers’ preferences and predict their reactions to ads.

    At the crux of the company is “the idea of bringing your strategy to life,” CEO and Founder Thor Olof Philogène told AdExchanger.

    Indeed, it’s the crux of the firm name: Stravito is a portmanteau of the words “strategy” and “vito,” which comes from the Latin word for life, “vita.”.

    In September, it rolled out its AI Persona Builder product, which uses brands’ data to develop AI personas that reflect their audiences.

    Stravito connects to a brand’s first-party data as well as other sources, like surveys and syndicated research, plus Stravito’s data from prior campaigns. From there, it builds out different AI personas for different audiences. The personas can represent smaller, more niche audiences, like people from a specific geo to capture “regional nuances,” said Philogène, or broader audiences, like millennials or Gen Z. Marketers can ask a persona a specific question, like why they prefer one version of an ad over another, “and get instant feedback,” he added.

    Industry observers note that coffee brand Lavazza, for instance, conducted several thousand consumer interviews that it was able to integrate into the personas it built with Stravito. When Lavazza was testing different styles of packaging for its Dolcevita line of coffee, it was able to get feedback on the different variations from a relevant customer persona.

    For this particular launch, Lavazza tested its US audience persona, which was built on data, including roughly 5,000 consumer interviews conducted through Kantar and research by the National Coffee Association. The research “covered consumers’ broader attitudes toward life, not only their attitudes toward coffee,” said Philogène, which helped with aesthetic decisions.

    Recent findings suggest that based on the persona’s responses to the colors and other visual cues, Lavazza ultimately changed the packaging color from black to dark blue, Philogène mentioned. It then validated the decision by testing the fresh designs on Meta and comparing engagement.

    But rather than just spitting out recommendations and hoping that marketers will trust the personas’ responses at face value, Stravito takes a “glass box” approach to AI, said Philogène. This means that every suggestion and piece of feedback that the AI generates is accompanied by the specific sources and citations that informed it.

    When your boss asks why you’re making a certain investment, “you do not want to tell them, you know, because AI told me so,” quipped Philogène. Instead, Stravito backs up its decision with the data sources it’s connected to.

    According to recent reports, but no matter how much research a brand or tech vendor has access to, no AI tool can accurately answer every question that someone may pose. And Stravito is exceedingly aware of that. Before a user even asks a question, said Philogène, the AI persona will note topics that it doesn’t have enough data to answer questions about, such as a brand’s pricing model.

    An AI tool’s lack of knowledge can be “a feature, not a bug,” remarked Philogène. It’s crucial for brands to understand what data they’re lacking and where they should commission extra data, he added.

    Sources indicate that stravito’s AI “won’t be sycophantic” and just tell users what they want to hear, stated Philogène. (Take that, ChatGPT.) Rather, it first determines whether or not it has enough data to answer a given question, and if it does, it specifies whether the answer is explicitly stated in the original source versus inferred. That way, the user can understand the logic backing up every one of the model’s conclusions.

    It has been revealed that having the necessary sources to back up one’s claims and decisions is a crucial facet of journalism, law and research, Philogène mentioned. Shouldn’t advertising be held to the same standard?

    Latest Update: OpenAI’s New Shopping Strategy; What Advertisers Are Thankful For

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.
    • So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.
    • The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.

    So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.

    The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”.

    The cynical take is that OpenAI is now allowing room for marketing partnerships to influence ChatGPT’s product recommendations, even outside of official ads.

    Sources indicate that other changes to the documentation are less important, though telling. ChatGPT formerly committed to showing products with “links to sites where you can learn more or purchase.” Now ChatGPT’s mandate is only to “show available ways to purchase.”.

    Recent findings suggest that marketers and merchants want to influence how their products and brands are presented to AI search consumers. There’s massive demand for such services (which are called AEO or GEO, as an evolution of SEO).

    Industry observers note that plus, some platforms that are essential for AI training are monetizing their influence over the chatbots. Amazon recently launched “Conversational Briefs” – a silly underwear-adjacent name for a product that lets brands pay to affect relevant AI search outputs.

    According to recent reports, but AI platforms themselves are hesitant to break the dam and let brands pay to boost their profile directly. Which could look like, for instance, businesses picking and choosing which customer reviews get surfaced or considered by the model, or pay-to-play prompts or keywords.

    Holiday ads might be creeping into the schedule earlier than ever this year, but don’t get it twisted: For a lot of TV advertisers, broadcasters and streamers, Thanksgiving weekend is the main event.

    On Thursday, NBCUniversal has the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the National Dog Show and one of three Thanksgiving NFL games (CBS and Fox will broadcast the other two). Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Netflix has the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game, and Prime Video is airing its first Duke men’s college basketball game. Then, on Black Friday, Prime has a 15-hour marathon of live sports coverage lined up, including an NFL game, two Emirates NBA Cup games and a PGA golf event.

    All that TV makes this weekend a crucial one for advertisers. Not only are many more people watching live during the Thanksgiving weekend (a record 34 million watched the Macy’s parade last year), but the National Retail Federation estimates that 182.7 million are planning to shop then, too.

    Which means it’s one of the rare times when TV is both a massive brand awareness play and short-term performance driver.

    It’s no wonder, then, that both NBC and Amazon are leaning heavily into interactive ad formats for their streaming broadcasts this year, as Variety reports. Amazon’s ads will feature on-screen prompts for interacting with Alexa or adding items straight to a customer’s Amazon cart, while Peacock will present shoppable pause ads that set up Instacart deliveries for customers.

    Ruh-roh: Loads of ad dollars are still getting lost in the programmatic abyss.

    Only 43.1% of programmatic spend made it to “quality media” last quarter, according to the latest ANA Programmatic Transparency Benchmark report. The research notes that, for every $1 million of programmatic ad spend, more than half is lost to transaction costs ($285,000) and media productivity ($284,000).

    According to recent reports, ad tech taxes aren’t solely to blame for the wasted spend, though. The lack of effective measurement is also a significant source of programmatic inefficiency, according to the ANA. And poor measurement standards are a “particularly acute” problem in connected TV environments, where a whopping 24% of ad spend went to “non-measurable inventory.”.

    While the report doesn’t clearly define what makes inventory non-measurable, it’s no secret that CTV ad measurement is murky, to say the very least. Publishers, agencies and measurement and currency vendors can hardly agree on how to count reach, let alone how to quantify outcomes.

    Sounds like those buy-side demands for more transparency are about to get even louder.

    Sources indicate that would you watch a 24/7 personalized AI TV channel about yourself? Because Google’s trying to patent that technology right now. [404 Media].

    Don’t write off DSPs in the age of agentic advertising. [Adweek].

    In a recent development, microsoft search advertisers can now extend their campaigns into the Pinterest search platform. [Ad Age].

    Recent findings suggest that after Jensen Huang’s unceremonious departure from NVIDIA amid affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple subordinates, the company has appointed its fresh CEO: Jensen Huang. [TechCrunch].

    Industry observers note that agentic advertising platform BrandComms.ai promotes Sheona Richard from chief client officer to CEO. [post].

    According to recent reports, CX platform Emplifi appoints Claire Wilson as chief marketing officer. [blog].

    Black Friday is almost here, and platforms are eager to claim their share of the shopping frenzy—and hopefully replicate the success TikTok Shop has seen over the last two years.

    In 2024, creators hosted over 30,000 live shopping streams on TikTok Shop—and some walked away with millions in sales. Stormi Steele, founder/CEO of hair/skincare brand Canvas Beauty, spotlighted her own brand in a TikTok livestream on Black Friday and made more than $2 million from viewers buying products off the broadcast.

    Canvas Beauty itself ended up selling 100,000+ products and making $3 million in sales over the course of the day, it told Business Insider.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Recent findings suggest that that trend picked up speed in 2025, with sellers and creators hosting over 760,000 livestream sessions across TikTok Shop’s Black Friday/Cyber Monday campaign (per TikTok). By hauling in over $500 million of U.S. sales between Black Friday and Cyber Monday, the ecommerce hub averaged over $125 million of daily sales across the four-day period.

    Sources indicate that tikTok, of course, is hoping to top that performance in 2026—and it seems well on its way to pulling it off. The platform reported that U.S. live shopping sales on Shop more than doubled in the first half of this year (as compared to the first half of 2025), and TikTok Shop President for Strategic Initiatives Patrick Nommensen added that hashtags like #holidayshopping rose 263% in September.

    Shop’s 2026 Black Friday/Cyber Monday holiday campaign began November 11 and is set to run until November 30, with top brands like Best Buy, Ulta Beauty, Sephora, Michael Kors, and Victoria’s Secret expected to take part (per Retail Brew).

    In a recent development, to keep viewers locked in on its Black Friday offerings, TikTok Shop will need to compete with Facebook Marketplace and Instagram, which eMarketer states dominate roughly three-quarters of U.S. social commerce.

    That’s a significant lead, but Meta isn’t resting on its laurels. Last week, Instagram introduced a new tool that lets creators add Amazon affiliate links directly to Reels and feed posts. As reported by Business Insider, an additional integration allows creators to link to products from Halara, Lowe’s and Shein.

    In a recent development, youTube is heading into its first holiday season with Amazon in its Shopping affiliate program, too. Since late August, eligible U.S. creators have been able to tag products from the ecommerce juggernaut in their Shorts, long-form videos, and livestreams.

    Recent findings suggest that not to be left out of the Black Friday push, Whatnot has unveiled intends to drop its sales cut to the “lowest level of the year,” with 0% commission for all sellers on Black Friday and again for eligible small sellers on November 28. Major creator collabs will also draw viewers to the live shopping platform, with MrBeast, Shay Mitchell, Kai Cenat, Claudia Oshry, Ben Soffer, David Dobrik, and other top stars hosting exclusive shows from November 27-30.

    Whatnot’s announcement post includes a blurb detailing “why Black Friday is better on Whatnot for shoppers”—but we’ll be keeping an eye out to see which platform actually comes out on top once the weekend wraps up.

    Google just filed a patent for a future without content creators

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google, which makes billions of dollars a year thanks to YouTubers stocking its platform with billions of hours of videos, is envisioning a future where we don’t need content creators.
    • According to 404 Media, the tech giant has filed a patent for something called “My Channel“: a 24/7 feed of AI-generated videos tailored specifically to every individual user’s preferences.
    • If put into practice, Google would take everything it knows about a person–which, between Google’s far-reaching ad biz, Android phones, Google Maps, and YouTube watch history, is a lot–and get (presumably) Veo to spool out an endless stream of content.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google, which makes billions of dollars a year thanks to YouTubers stocking its platform with billions of hours of videos, is envisioning a future where we don’t need content creators.

    According to 404 Media, the tech giant has filed a patent for something called “My Channel“: a 24/7 feed of AI-generated videos tailored specifically to every individual user’s preferences.

    If put into practice, Google would take everything it knows about a person–which, between Google’s far-reaching ad biz, Android phones, Google Maps, and YouTube watch history, is a lot–and get (presumably) Veo to spool out an endless stream of content.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    It has been revealed that but we’re not just talking any content. Google’s key selling point here is that you–yes, you–can star in all of your slop channel’s videos.

    Recent findings suggest that “You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist,” Google claims in an example prompt filed with the patent application. “The generated customized video includes characteristics based on the . The generated customized video follows the style and format of the of the user. The generated customized video sticks to the of the user but the narrative for the generated customized video is customized. The and parameters are ordered from more preferred to less preferred.”.

    404 Media reports the patent notes My Channels will be connected to an “advertising server” that will “[generate] an updated customized media content item by inserting at least one advertisement into the customized media content item.”.

    Basically, it wants to put a fake you into fake videos as their “protagonist,” and then you’ll have to watch real ads to see the fake you in the fake videos.

    In a recent development, does this necessarily mean everyone who has a My Channel will stop watching human creators? No. But a 24/7 channel of customized catnip will drain at least some watch time toward these siloed slop-factories, and away from humans who make actual content (and rely on views for income).

    As for the sorts of videos Google’s AI will generate, the patent filing included examples like “a crime/comedy caper,” “a fun romantic comedy,” “a sci-fi adventure,” and “an action/thriller experience,” all of which would be slopped out for a viewer named “John.”.

    In a recent development, in another example, the “protagonist” is a viewer who likes cricket. If Google’s system noticed this person watching a video about a certain player’s gangbuster performance during a recent cricket match, it could then generate a video “that incorporates elements of the Cricket World Cup and Player 1’s recent performance,” the filing says. “Perhaps [user_name] could be cheering for India in the stands or interacting with Player 1 in some way.”.

    As 404 Media points out, numerous proponents of gen AI have spent years crowing about the potential for personalized entertainment. Didn’t like how Stranger Things ended? Generate your ending. Third movie in a series got cancelled? Just ‘make’ it yourself. News coverage didn’t agree with your opinion? Your chatbot’s ready with a new broadcast. It sounds dystopian, because it is. It also seemed far-fetched, three years ago.

    This is a future we’ve already been pitched. It’s just that once, the pitch was a Black Mirror episode. Now it’s Google’s business model.

    #227564. Principal Media Or Unprincipled Media?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (517 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Principal Media Or Unprincipled Media?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.
    • It’s a head-scratcher, states Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.
    • “Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he indicates.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.

    It’s a head-scratcher, states Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.

    “Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he indicates.

    It has been revealed that in a principal media deal, an agency isn’t just advising a client; it’s selling to them. The agency buys media in bulk with its own money, then resells it to the client – usually without saying what’s in the package or what it paid – and then keeps the difference.

    Which raises an obvious question: Is the agency recommending what’s best for its client or what’s best for the agency?

    It has been revealed that to understand how the industry got here, Asghar notes, you have to go back around 25 years to when media buying was unbundled at the behest of procurement and agencies started pooling client dollars to gain leverage. The original idea was to pass along the savings.

    But after the ANA’s K2 report came out in 2016, it became clear that agencies were holding onto major volume rebates for themselves.

    “They’re not actually savings; they’re profit,” Asghar says. “And they’re about the purest form of profit a organization could attribute to their bottom line.”.

    In a recent development, today, holding companies have repackaged those rebates as principal deals, which is really just arbitrage. Asghar argues that this money should go back to the client.

    Not that any of this is happening secretly, though. Defenders of principal media like to say it’s fine as long as clients opt in. But Asghar isn’t buying it.

    Recent findings suggest that “It’s one thing to know it’s happening,” he indicates. “It’s another thing to know what’s happening inside of what’s happening.”.

    In other words, marketers can sign off on a principal deal and still have no idea what ended up on the proposal. They often can’t get log-level data showing where their ads ran or what they originally cost. And because agencies buy the inventory at undisclosed discounts or through volume rebates before reselling it at a markup, the true price is hidden.

    Marketers should go back to buying media separately from planning and strategy services, Asghar says, so the agencies giving advice aren’t also the ones with inventory to move.

    Otherwise, Asghar states, an agency isn’t really acting as an agent.

    Being a fiduciary, he notes, “means you have a responsibility to do what’s in the best interest of [clients], not just what’s in the best interest of you or your shareholders.”.

    Also in this episode: Why AI is going to “make dumb companies dumber and smart companies exceptional,” why young planners still need to learn the old-fashioned way even if agents can do some of their work for them and why attribution and measurement are the “dry turkey” of ad tech. (It “looks great on the outside,” Asghar quips, “but it’s terrible on the inside.”).

    • Now, Roblox is switching gears from horror to family-friendly holiday fun.
    • Starting tomorrow, the sandbox platform will kick off The Great Build: a global community event culminating in the creation of “a massive tower of gratitude.” According to a press release, the event will run through Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last month, Roblox ushered in Halloween with a platform-wide horror event stocked with mazes, monsters, and general mayhem. That nine-night event—called The Hollow—featured creepy creatures from a variety of well-known Roblox experiences, including 99 Nights in the Forest, DOORS, Dandy’s World, Scary Shawarma Kiosk, and more.

    Now, Roblox is switching gears from horror to family-friendly holiday fun. Ahead of Thanksgiving, the platform is inviting players to express their gratitude by building something tall—“like, really tall.”.

    Starting tomorrow, the sandbox platform will kick off The Great Build: a global community event culminating in the creation of “a massive tower of gratitude.” According to a press release, the event will run through Nov. 30 and is designed to encourage players around the world to “share what they’re thankful for and work together toward a shared goal.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, the process is as simple as it is wholesome. Every hour, players will receive a free block that they can personalize with a message “inspired by gratitude traditions from around the world” and add to the tower, Roblox says.

    Players can also climb The Great Build as it grows, and will unlock free avatar items as different community milestones are achieved.

    A gratitude-themed event aimed at global unity is exactly the kind of positive PR Roblox needs right now.

    According to Latin Times, the sandbox platform is currently facing almost 200 consolidated federal lawsuits, with states and parents alike pushing back against the platform’s approach to child safety.

    Legislators are bearing down on Roblox, too. Earlier this month, Senators Josh Hawley and Dick Durbin proposed the “No Forced Arbitration for Child Sexual Exploitation and Cyber Injuries Act,” which would allow families to take Roblox to court regardless of forced arbitration terms.

    The “first-ever congressional hearing on Roblox safety” followed the bill’s introduction and included appearances from both legal experts and survivors of child sexual exploitation.

    Roblox CEO David Baszucki, on the other hand, reportedly sent a “last-minute letter instead of testifying before the Senate subcommittee.” We’re guessing the platform’s Thanksgiving tower of gratitude won’t be quite tall enough to overshadow that absence.

    #227558. Latest Update: Healthcare Ads Are Coming To ChatGPT

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (876 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Healthcare Ads Are Coming To ChatGPT

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When OpenAI announced in January that ChatGPT would soon be serving ads, it emphasized that, for early testing, ads were “not eligible to appear near sensitive or regulated topics like health, mental health or politics,” and healthcare ads were entirely prohibited.
    • But as OpenAI’s ads business matures, it’s begun to expand what content ads can served against, as well as which advertisers it permits ads from.
    • On Tuesday, WebMD Ignite, the healthcare enterprise division of WebMD, announced its ChatGPT ads offering.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When OpenAI announced in January that ChatGPT would soon be serving ads, it emphasized that, for early testing, ads were “not eligible to appear near sensitive or regulated topics like health, mental health or politics,” and healthcare ads were entirely prohibited.

    But as OpenAI’s ads business matures, it’s begun to expand what content ads can served against, as well as which advertisers it permits ads from.

    On Tuesday, WebMD Ignite, the healthcare enterprise division of WebMD, announced its ChatGPT ads offering.

    WebMD Ignite serves hospitals and healthcare providers with agency solutions as well as content and data solutions, including its own DSP. Now, its agency offerings will include the opportunity to launch ads in ChatGPT.

    ChatGPT Ads’ most recent ad policies provide more explicit detail on what is and isn’t permitted within healthcare advertising and offer more leeway than before. At least, there’s more leeway in the US – heath-related ads are still “generally prohibited” in other countries, according to the policy.

    The ad policy also states that regulated products and services are still prohibited writ large, as are “claims related to the prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of physical or mental health conditions.”.

    However, OpenAI may accept ads on a case-by-case basis for less regulated offerings, including hospital and urgent care, health insurance, dietary supplements and consumer medical devices, wearables and apps.

    Of WebMD Ignite’s clients, OpenAI has thus far only permitted ads from health systems and providers (like hospitals and academic medical centers), but not insurance companies.

    According to recent reports, over 30% of Americans have used AI chatbots for health advice or information, so medical providers want to ensure that they’re “present and discoverable” within LLMs, mentioned Ann Bilyew, president of WebMD Ignite. Ads are a seemingly straightforward way to achieve that presence.

    Sources indicate that the problem, noted Bilyew, is that most of them aren’t sure how best to design the creative and messaging in a way that will let them through the “gates” of OpenAI. WebMD Ignite works directly with OpenAI, and so has more insight into the protocol and standards. “As we learn something for one health system, we’re able to apply it to all the others,” said Bilyew.

    It’s too early to assert any definitive learnings, but WebMD Ignite believes that “contextual alignment will be a critical driver of performance,” Nora Simmons, VP of activation strategy, told AdExchanger.

    ChatGPT has a “relatively constrained creative format” that, for the moment, consists of an image, the brand name and a brief message, said Simmons, and doesn’t allow for particularly unique ad formats. As a result, she said, it’s particularly crucial to ensure that the ad’s message – and then the landing page, if a user clicks on the ad – matches the intent of the user’s conversation.

    According to recent reports, it’s also crucial that the ad is “informational, not promotional,” mentioned Bilyew – though she acknowledged that the line between the two can be quite blurry. Generally speaking, informational ads can include specific examples of the services offered, locations and any certifications and awards they’ve received.

    Healthcare marketers also aren’t immune to the challenges that all ChatGPT advertisers face: namely, knowing what sort of queries their ads appear against.

    Clients can see data on views and clicks, mentioned Bilyew, but not on the specific content (or even types of content) that their ads appear next to. This is particularly challenging for healthcare advertisers, since ads are prohibited from appearing in any health-related conversations that are deemed sensitive or personal, making it more difficult to predict what queries they can show up against.

    Determining what makes a conversation too sensitive for advertising is a subjective metric, but OpenAI told AdExchanger that even if a health condition is “strongly implied,” rather than explicitly stated, ads won’t be served during the conversation. “Someone does not need to explicitly name a diagnosis or ask for medical treatment for a conversation to fall into that sensitive category,” mentioned OpenAI.

    For now, WebMD Ignite is optimizing its clients’ ads for informative content that doesn’t directly refer to the user’s own health conditions, such as queries like, “I’m looking to understand heart health,” said Bilyew.

    Industry observers note that webMD Ignite also needs to have different versions of an ad for different contexts. For instance, Simmons mentioned, a cardiology center would want to offer different messaging to someone looking to find a cardiologist versus someone asking specific questions about a particular cardiac procedure. It’s been testing roughly 100 creative variations in its early work with the cardiology division of an academic medical center, with “different messages, conversational contexts and geographic markets,” she added.

    But one of WebMD Ignite’s greatest strengths is its willingness to admit how little is known about AI search advertising at this early stage. “We don’t know what a good budget should be in a given region,” mentioned Bilyew, or what the delivery or inventory will look like. “We’re starting with very defined tests,” she added, and comparing the results to paid search to start assessing budget allocation on a larger scale.

    “Our message to clients is, ‘Look, just get in there and start learning,’” Bilyew remarked. “Then, as things evolve, you’ll be in a good position to evolve with it.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that but the overall-clad creator isn’t just helping tots reach their learning milestones online—she’s also advocating for children caught up in the U.S. immigration system.

    On Monday, Ms Rachel (aka Rachel Accurso) joined U.S. Representative-elect Brad Lander at an immigration court in New York City to support children expected to take part in legal hearings without attorneys.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In a recent development, accurso posted a video of the visit on Instagram, where she wrote that “Kids representing themselves in immigration court is so wrong… I saw Angel up at the mic without a lawyer and I couldn’t believe it. He’s 9 years old! Hearing kids hear the word ‘removable’ over and over about themselves… Heartbreaking.”.

    A nine-year-old appearing in court without a lawyer may seem unfathomable, but Angel is far from the only child representing himself within a deeply complicated immigration system.

    Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, the Trump administration failed to renew a contract “with a nationwide network of legal service providers that represented thousands of unaccompanied minors in immigration court” (per the Times Union). While Governor Kathy Hochul confirmed state funding to combat the sudden gap in resources, New York still has “the third-largest unaccompanied minors caseload in the nation” with nearly 10,000 open cases as of August 2026.

    As severe as New York’s backlog is, it’s just one part of a nationwide crisis—and Accurso isn’t limiting her advocacy to the East Coast.

    Just a few days before appearing at the Ted Weiss Federal Building in NYC, the creator used her expansive online platform to spotlight a conversation with Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa. In a video shared on Instagram, Hinojosa shared her blueprint to end family immigration detention—a cause Accurso herself has vocally championed.

    Advocacy on multiple fronts has long been a key part of Accurso’s online presence, despite repeated backlash from right-wing critics and parents over her support for the LGBTQ+ community and Palestinian children impacted by the war in Gaza.

    The creator’s contributions to the latter cause include a 2024 campaign that raised $50,000 for Save the Children’s Emergency Fund and, more recently, a $1 million pledge to the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund.

    According to recent reports, now, as Accurso fights for the rights of minors in U.S. courtrooms and detention centers, she’s demonstrating once again that all children are welcome in Ms Rachel’s classroom.

    #227552. Amazon Can’t Quit ChatGPT; Manipulative Mobile Game Ads Win

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (855 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    Amazon Can’t Quit ChatGPT; Manipulative Mobile Game Ads Win

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that happy Thanksgiving!
    • Name two bigger frenemies in ecommerce than OpenAI and Amazon.
    • The two companies are headed for a showdown over online shopping, argues Mike Shields at Next in Media.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that happy Thanksgiving! The AdExchanger team will be taking the rest of the week off to enjoy the holiday. The Daily News Roundup will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

    Name two bigger frenemies in ecommerce than OpenAI and Amazon.

    The two companies are headed for a showdown over online shopping, argues Mike Shields at Next in Media. But they also can’t completely cut each other off from their respective platforms without threatening potential sales.

    The retail media model, which Amazon has perfected, works because it’s easy to connect ads to purchases, Shields writes. But when chatbot-based research becomes part of the customer journey, the path from ad exposure to final transaction gets much harder to trace. Just look at the IAB’s upcoming convoluted AI attribution framework, which does what it can to try and account for the many ways AI can influence a purchase.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, Amazon realizes OpenAI is trying to steal its lunch. That’s why Amazon blocks OpenAI crawlers from accessing its retail site and prevents ChatGPT ads from linking directly to Amazon product listings.

    But not even Amazon could resist the urge to advertise on ChatGPT during the holiday shopping season, Digiday reports.

    Industry observers note that that creates an awkward situation for Amazon, however. Its restrictions on OpenAI are also impacting how its own ad attribution works. For instance, Amazon’s ChatGPT ads direct shoppers to complete their purchase on Amazon’s site. But because they can’t click through to the product page, they have to click through to search results instead.

    And, because OpenAI can’t scrape Amazon’s site or its product pages directly, ChatGPT has to analyze info sourced from third-party deal-tracking sites to give shoppers useful advice.

    Good luck to the measurement platforms trying to make any sense of all this!

    Most readers may not recognize the mobile game Gossip Harbor. But its social and mobile video ads are hard to miss: horrific AI-generated scenes of marital infidelity, child neglect and animal abuse, alongside strange calls-to-action involving scenes like a mother and daughter freezing in a collapsing shelter.

    The trend of AI-generated crisis ads has been covered at length, and there’s a whole economy of mobile games that redirect the resulting traffic to unrelated titles. It sounds like an implausible business model – but the numbers tell a different story.

    Sensor Tower and GameRefinery data show Gossip Harbor climbing the revenue rankings in Apple’s App Store and Google Play this year. By November, its monthly in-app revenue had topped even Candy Crush’s roughly $100 million. Mobile growth consultant Matej Lancaric has a blog post detailing the game’s revenue and marketing strategy.

    Aside from its ghastly creative approach, Gossip Harbor is one of the biggest games in the mobile category. What is that, you might ask? In many popular mobile merge games, players keep progressing through an ongoing story on a persistent board instead of clearing one level after another. The game is designed to go on indefinitely with regular updates.

    The ads prey on people’s anxiety to attract players, and then the games monetize the attention that follows.

    Black Friday deals just don’t hit the same way they once did – and not only because fewer people are willing to get into parking lot fistfights over them.

    Part of the problem, Marketing Brew argues, is that the savings are no longer relegated to a single day. Extending Black Friday into an entire month not only eases the fear of missing out, but also creates something called “promotion fatigue,” where customers are unsure about the right time to buy and may end up buying less as a result.

    On top of the constant deals, customers have also become generally less trusting that they’re actually getting a bargain during the holiday season. Which makes sense because, oftentimes, they’re not.

    As watchdog group Groundwork Collective recently found, some retailers advertise Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals that don’t offer any significant savings. Others, meanwhile, reserve cheaper, lower-quality inventory specifically to sell during Black Friday, especially electronics.

    In a recent development, so how should advertisers approach Black Friday shopping campaigns? Well, actually making the deals worthwhile would go a long way, for starters. For some companies, that might include staggering which products go on sale and when or ensuring that the prices are meaningfully low.

    Or you could just forgo the Black Friday rhetoric entirely and focus on brand-building instead, of course.

    In a recent development, tidal bans AI-generated music from its platform entirely and will remove 29 million AI songs, claiming that 96% of AI tracks receive zero plays. Tidal already demonetized all AI-generated songs five months ago. [Variety].

    During an all-hands meeting discussing his comeback, returning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang claims the organization will hire a compliance officer “for the first time.” [post].

    Sources indicate that private equity firm RedBird Capital Partners has finalized its purchase of a majority stake in Puck, a digital news publisher. [The Wrap].

    According to recent reports, writer, podcaster and events host Alex Konrad is making his small media business work by focusing on startup founders and ventures. [Inc.].

    #227548. Tech Report: Thumbnails help YouTubers build audiences. Now everyone can put custom ‘nails on their Shorts.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (477 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Thumbnails help YouTubers build audiences. Now everyone can put custom ‘nails on their Shorts.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that you get a thumbnail.
    • That’s right: YouTube has, at long, long last, finally allowed all creators to assign customized thumbnails to their Shorts.
    • In a recent development, when YouTube introduced Shorts in 2020, they were its attempt to keep up with TikTok.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that you get a thumbnail. And you get a thumbnail! And you . . .

    That’s right: YouTube has, at long, long last, finally allowed all creators to assign customized thumbnails to their Shorts.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In a recent development, when YouTube introduced Shorts in 2020, they were its attempt to keep up with TikTok. TikTok didn’t offer custom thumbnails, because its whole platform is based on endless scrolling. The thought process was that if short-form videos did have thumbnails, people wouldn’t really see them, because videos are discovered by swiping up, not by visiting a creator’s profile.

    It has been revealed that but we all know that viewers do visit creators’ profiles. Not only do thumbnails–for long- or short-form–help a creator define their visual style and personal brand, but unique thumbnails help repeat viewers identify videos they’ve watched (and also, as a bonus plus, keep creators from being stuck with a perhaps unflattering moment as their content’s hero image).

    Sources indicate that tikTok later caved and added thumbnails to short-form videos. But YouTube, Land of Thumbnails, did not–at least, not until this past summer.

    In July, YouTube introduced custom Shorts thumbnails for everyone in the YouTube Partner Program, with YouTube CEO Neal Mohan saying custom thumbnails were “one of the most requested features” for the platform.

    You loved custom Shorts thumbnails—now every creator can use them on desktop and mobile!

    ✏️ Tap the pencil icon on any Short in @YouTube Studio to upload yours.

    — Neal Mohan (@nealmohan) November 23, 2026.

    YouTube’s thumbnail selection tool allowed creators to add their own images, just like with long-form videos, but also offers a TikTok-esque option where it’ll select a few screenshots from within the video and offer them as default thumbnails, for anyone who doesn’t want to apply YouTube-effort editing to their short-form content.

    There’s one important thing to note from the July announcement, though: Shorts thumbnails went out to all YouTube Partner Program creators. Not to everyone–including any creators who are trying to drum up enough viewership to become a Partner creator.

    It has been revealed that this is a big flip from 2024, when YouTube outright remarked it didn’t think Shorts thumbnails could be as impactful as long-form thumbnails. And, look, we get it: Shorts thumbnails vs long-form thumbnails is sort of like putting a half-page up against a full spread, to put things in publication terms. Shorts thumbnails inherently offer less room to work with, and thus less room to communicate videos’ vibes.

    But half-pages are still vital in the grand scheme, and considering how much watch time Shorts drives for YouTube and for creators, they should have the same audience engagement and brand identity tools as long-form content.

    #227547. What Does ‘Performance’ Actually Mean for TV? Buyers Weigh In

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (881 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    What Does ‘Performance’ Actually Mean for TV? Buyers Weigh In

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you’re a TV campaign planner or media buyer, you probably hear the words “outcomes” and “performance” more than phrases like “how are you?” Sad, but true.
    • But what does performance actually mean in TV environments?
    • It has been revealed that these two questions were the focus of a panel of buyers at this year’s Go Addressable event in New York City on Thursday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you’re a TV campaign planner or media buyer, you probably hear the words “outcomes” and “performance” more than phrases like “how are you?” Sad, but true.

    But what does performance actually mean in TV environments? And what do media buyers need to achieve that performance?

    It has been revealed that these two questions were the focus of a panel of buyers at this year’s Go Addressable event in New York City on Thursday. Go Addressable is a nonprofit trade organization focused on advancing addressable TV advertising.

    According to recent reports, different advertisers typically have their own metrics for defining performance, ranging from reach and brand awareness to purchase consideration and real-life sales. But what buyers agree on is the belief that brand awareness and performance are not only connected, but causal.

    When it comes to TV and video ads, “if we don’t have scalable audiences, we can’t drive outcomes,” said Maureen Bosetti, chief investment officer at Omnicom Media Group, speaking on a panel taking place on the Go Addressable stage.

    Recent findings suggest that in other words: The entirety of the marketing funnel matters when running TV ads that aim to move money – not just lower-funnel numbers like retail sales. Hence the renewed prevalence of the term “full-funnel” in TV advertising discussions, including during this year’s upfront season.

    According to recent reports, improved measurement and transparency are at the top of buyers’ wish lists to help make TV ads work as desired. Hopefully publishers and their intermediaries will listen this time.

    When it comes to measuring video ad outcomes, the TV industry is setting itself up for disappointment because we “oversimplify” the human nature of viewers, said Jennifer Gardner, chief client solutions officer at Carat US, a subsidiary of dentsu, speaking on the same panel.

    In a recent development, no matter how many QR codes and calls to action advertisers slap onto ad creatives, TV is still a lean-back viewing environment. At least compared with other channels and personal devices used for online shopping, such as cell phones, laptops and tablets.

    In a recent development, generally speaking, TV viewers are not going to immediately pick up their phones or pause their show to run to the store when they see a commercial advertising an interesting product, Gardner stated. More often than not, viewers store that information to look into later, when they’re not in the middle of the show.

    According to recent reports, seeing a brand’s advertised product in the wild over time also plays a role in persuading viewers to buy something they remember seeing on TV, Gardner added. “Purchase behavior is heavily influenced by mindset,” she mentioned, “which is built over time.”.

    Plus, performance encompasses more than just sales. Different category verticals have their own preferred outcomes they use to gauge performance.

    Industry observers note that for example, fast-food and quick-service restaurants (QSR) often prioritize incremental reach as their preferred metric of performance, Bosetti said. For QSR brands, reach drives foot traffic, which drives business, she said, noting that QSR brands often plan media based on channels and platform most likely to reach, say, households with young children who frequent fast-food restaurants multiple times per week.

    In other words, Bosetti remarked, an upper-funnel play can also be a performance-driven one.

    Despite the variances in how brands define outcomes – and how long it takes for TV to have an impact on driving those outcomes – agencies agree they need better measurement and transparency.

    Conversations pushing for better measurement and transparency have been ongoing for multiple grueling years (can confirm). Years of demands and effort toward that pursuit have led to a renewed rise in marketing mix modeling (MMM) and piecemeal upgrades in content transparency across certain publishers and their tech partners.

    Upgrades are cool. But according to agencies, they’re not enough.

    MMM is valuable, Gardner said, but it is “backward-looking” and “doesn’t tell you about changes happening in the future,” which makes it difficult for marketers to use insights from MMM before it’s too late.

    Agencies need more than just MMM to measure and optimize campaigns.

    Sources indicate that what agencies need, Bosetti noted, is standardized and “holistic” measurement that gives buyers a comprehensive view of customers and their consumption behaviors across channels, from broadcast TV and streaming to social media and online video. That comprehensive view, she said, is a core component to agencies’ ability to spot opportunities for cost-cutting and improved ad effectiveness.

    Transparency is also an notable part of the ad measurement equation.

    According to recent reports, A lot of media aims have “dead reach,” Gardner mentioned, which agencies can mitigate if they have a better understanding of their target consumers. That comprehensive understanding goes beyond just audience signals and identity resolution, though, she said. According to Gardner, agencies need more detailed data from sell-side partners that capture content signals and attention data.

    Agencies want publishers to cough up more information about what viewers are actually watching and what they’re paying most attention to.

    It has been revealed that but will they? Won’t they? Or will more debates over measurement and transparency continue to be the object of a tug-of-war game between agencies and publishers?

    Only time will tell, but don’t worry – we’re keeping close watch on this space.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (479 w)

    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    On OnlyFans, one-time transactions are winning out over subscriptions

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (479 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that back in August, OnlyFans confirmed that 5,076 creators have brought in at least $1 million each since the NSFW hub kicked off in 2016, with total creator payouts adding up to $30 billion.
    • That last figure represents a solid increase in how much creators are making on OnlyFans—but the way they’re making money on the platform has evolved in recent years, too.
    • Industry observers note that according to a recent report from Giggster, the vast majority of the $6.2 billion paid to OnlyFans creators in 2025 stemmed from non-subscription-based transactions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that back in August, OnlyFans confirmed that 5,076 creators have brought in at least $1 million each since the NSFW hub kicked off in 2016, with total creator payouts adding up to $30 billion. About 20% of that $30 billion—roughly $6.2 billion—was delivered to creators during the year that ended on November 30, 2025.

    That last figure represents a solid increase in how much creators are making on OnlyFans—but the way they’re making money on the platform has evolved in recent years, too.

    Industry observers note that according to a recent report from Giggster, the vast majority of the $6.2 billion paid to OnlyFans creators in 2025 stemmed from non-subscription-based transactions. To compile its report (titled “Behind the OnlyFans Paycheck: Creator Payments, Platform Fees and U.S. Rankings”), the online marketplace combined “illustrative payment calculations with third-party estimates of OnlyFans creator accounts across all 50 states and Washington, D.C.” and examined “manufacturer-level revenue by payment type and revenue attributed to the U.S.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    In a recent development, overall, the report estimated that 700,000 OnlyFans creator accounts are active in the U.S., a number that makes up roughly 28% of the platform’s global total. And despite representing less than 30% of OnlyFans accounts, Giggster found that ~62% of OnlyFans’ platform revenue ($965.4 million) was attributed to the U.S. in the 2025 fiscal year.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the report’s most significant findings, however, relates to the rising importance of non-subscription-based revenue—aka payments from one-time transactions like tips, paywalled posts, paid direct messages, and custom content requests. According to Giggster, those payments generated 73% of OnlyFans’ platform revenue in the 2025 fiscal year (up from roughly 40% in 2020 and 60% in 2024).

    OnlyFans isn’t the only creator-driven platform leaning into one-time payments, either. In a 2024 end-of-year post, Patreon noted that creators on its platform “increased monthly revenue of one-time purchases by 4x” year-over-year. More recently, a study from Ipsos commissioned by TikTok predicted that over 60,000 U.S.-based TikTok LIVE creators would make “more than the median part-time monthly income” from gift earnings in 2025.

    According to recent reports, youTube has devoted significant resources to one-time transactions, too. In a January blog post, CEO Neal Mohan reassured creators that the video platform would “continue to invest” in “fan funding features like Jewels and gifts,” adding that “we know these are important revenue streams, especially outside the U.S., for creators like Santiago Matias, who uses Super Chat as a way for fans to influence the outcome of his hit reality series.”.

    At the end of the day, the rising importance of one-time transactions demonstrates an vital truth for creators: if you want to earn more revenue, give fans more ways to pay you.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Earlier this month, X launched a latest feature that allows owners to clip moments from their favorite videos, add their own takes, and hit post without leaving the platform.

    In theory, that tool (inventively named “Clipping”) is a win-win for everyone involved. Clips credit and link back to the original videos, and both original creators and clippers can earn revenue through X’s engagement-based creator rewards program (aka Original Content Rewards).

    X isn’t stopping there, though. On November 20, the platform shared that “video is the fastest growing format on X,” adding that “Posts with video get 5x the reach and engagement, and 36% of all impressions now go to video.”.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    According to recent reports, now, to build on that momentum, X has unveiled a fresh slate of video creation and streaming tools designed to help creators “produce polished vertical video without leaving” the platform. Those include….

    X is also beefing up monetization options for video creators. In addition to Original Content Rewards (which replaced the platform’s Revenue Sharing program earlier this fall), X has introduced Video Kickstart Bonus, “an invite-only pilot that pays creators a bonus for posting original vertical video under three minutes with no watermarks.”.

    It has been revealed that tikTok, of course, didn’t stay offline for very long—but that hasn’t stopped X from continuing to refine its video offerings. In February of this year, the platform rolled out a redesigned immersive player intended to make video more watchable on mobile.

    With its latest slate of video features and monetization options, X finally appears to be putting its money where its mouth is—and offering creators the tools they need to take advantage.

    In a recent development, speed wasn’t done. His latest video features him racing against the man, the myth, the legend: Usain Bolt. Clocking in at 11 million views in only 48 hours, this upload is on track to be one of his biggest videos to date.

    #227528. Everyone wants a piece of creator IPs. Outshine Talent founder Barbara Jones is making that work in her clients’ favor.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (968 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tubefilter ↗ Open Full Page

    Everyone wants a piece of creator IPs. Outshine Talent founder Barbara Jones is making that work in her clients’ favor.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tubefilter

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, creator IPs have been the talk of the town this year, and we don’t expect that to change as we head into 2027.
    • While much of the attention around this new media “gold rush” has focused on mainstream entertainment companies (finally) recognizing creators’ value, we think it’s equally as key to spotlight development efforts happening within established creator-space companies.
    • That’s why we chatted with Barbara Jones, who founded Outshine Talent in 2019.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, creator IPs have been the talk of the town this year, and we don’t expect that to change as we head into 2027. As you’ll know if you’re a regular Tubefilter reader, there are many creator IP projects in the works–some with major Hollywood studios, some with Netflix and Disney, some with smaller independent studios, and some produced entirely by creators themselves (maybe with a little help from YouTube?).

    While much of the attention around this new media “gold rush” has focused on mainstream entertainment companies (finally) recognizing creators’ value, we think it’s equally as key to spotlight development efforts happening within established creator-space companies.

    That’s why we chatted with Barbara Jones, who founded Outshine Talent in 2019. Prior to launching Outshine, Jones founded influencer marketing agency Intuition Media Group, where she spent 12 years, and also served as a founding board member of the Influencer Marketing Association.

    Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

    Jones recently expanded Outshine to a new arm, called Outshine Entertainment, that focuses on helping creators build original IPs across things like short films, microdramas, full-length films, and TV; it also produces live events. Outshine is encouraging its clients to take creative chances and make their dream projects, and is also encouraging studios and streamers that could offer financial and production support for those projects to get involved.

    Some of Outshine Entertainment’s current and prospective creator projects include:.

    It has been revealed that “It’s a natural evolution for a lot of these creators to say, ‘I want to do more,'” Jones says. “‘I’m a great writer, I’m a comedian, I’m an actor, I want to do more of these things.’ And I feel the industry is actually realizing the value and saying, ‘Yeah, I think you’re right. We need to start supporting these latest, fresh faces, fresh ideas, things that are maybe a little more inexpensive and worth taking a shot on, seeing what we can do.'”.

    Jones states she feels the atmosphere right now is ripe for creators to experiment, and to license out their production ideas to places like Tubi that are willing to take the ride with them. She believes creators keeping a relatively low production cost will spur companies to support them.

    In a recent development, “We’re filling the pipeline with originals and fresh ideas and things that don’t have to cost a fortune to try and test,” she says. “Creators have that ability to test things out, see where they go, and then expand upon them if something’s really, really going.”.

    It has been revealed that she points to the Romano Brothers series as an example. Sahid, Maystrik, and Hernandez originally created the series as a parody of popular love sibling-rivalry love triangles in shows like The Summer I Turned Pretty. They weren’t sure it would take off, but they threw it up on TikTok–and after a very enthusiastic reception from viewers, they committed to the idea and turned it into a full-fledged original series with Tubi.

    Industry observers note that successful creators tend to be inherently good at identifying what content resonates with their viewers, and how to build on that content’s themes and ideas to widen the scope and keep people coming back. That’s exactly what happened with Never Have I Ever Spent the Winter with the Romano Brothers.

    It has been revealed that “They had just done it for themselves,” Jones says. “But they realized it would turn into something because it had audience interest. And that’s the fun part about it. I always say to our talent: The gatekeepers are gone. You’ve just got to try it. Just make it. We can always find money. We can find resources. We can find those things, but everyone’s looking for fresh ideas, for ingenuity.”.

    She points to another plus of working with creators: They’re “speedboats” whereas traditional entertainment tends to be a “cruise ship.”.

    It has been revealed that with creators, “You can be quicker to try things,” she notes. “And, for the first time, I’m really feeling like there are outside forces that want to help creators fund some of these things.”.

    With that funding in hand, creators are “leveling up, because now these are productions versus being solo, making everything yourself,” Jones says.

    Some funding can come from brands, Jones thinks. “I was just talking to a brand at one of our events, and I was saying, Why aren’t we just doing a microdrama? Let’s just do a microdrama that has product placement in it, but is actually a fun storyline,” she claims. “That takes a normal sponsored post to the next level. We have to start thinking differently. I really believe creators are modern media, and I think people are catching up to that and realizing [a creator’s] audience is what they need to be focused on.”.

    We’ve already seen a few brands push in and build their own microdramas to advertise products. It’s not far-fetched at all to envision a world where Sahid, Maystrik, and Hernandez’s next parody project comes with a sponsor–maybe even one that’s willing to be a little self-aware and play along with the satire. Imagine a classic romcom “oh no, there’s only one bed and it’s snowing outside so we have to cuddle!” situation sponsored by a cozy sleepwear company, or a hot cocoa brand.

    Jones states supporting creators’ original IPs is a top priority for Outshine going into 2027.

    “It’s very exciting. I have a lot of young, fresh faces who are super creative and love to have ideas, and now I feel like I actually have places to bring them,” she says. “I have people who are really listening to what creators can do.”.

    I Blind-Tested 3 Gemini Models On Real SEO Questions – Neon Won 5 Of 6 via @sejournal, @marie_haynes

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.
    • Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s newly introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.
    • Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Over the last few months, I have been quietly building something I call Marie’s Brain – a private AI co-pilot grounded in my hand-curated Open Knowledge Format (OKF) library of Search and AI research.

    Recently, I switched the tool over to Google’s newly introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. After using it for a while, though, I had a nagging feeling: Is Hydrogen actually producing better answers than Gemini 3.8 Flash, or am I just assuming newer means better?

    Instead of guessing, I decided to run a real blind taste test – and threw Gemini 4 Neon into the mix too.

    You can actually try the exact same six-question blind test yourself here (columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every question, and there is a button at the top to reveal how I voted and the real token costs).

    The blind 3-way taste test interface: columns A, B, and C are shuffled on every SEO question, complete with clickable OKF concept pills. Try voting blind yourself here. Image Credit: Marie Haynes.

    Before I even finished reading the first round of blind outputs, one thing jumped out immediately: The answers were way too long.

    Industry observers note that my Brain had been defaulting to Detailed mode with no word ceiling. When we checked the API logs, we discovered something wild: Gemini 4 Hydrogen was going into an over-eager research loop, reading an average of 21 OKF files per question, taking 68 seconds, writing 1,600-word essays, and costing $0.44 per prompt – actually more expensive per turn than Gemini 4 Neon!

    On top of that, some answers were dropping internal Google engineering jargon (like MAGIT and FastSearch) that a busy business owner does not need to wade through just to figure out why their clicks dropped.

    So before doing my real blind vote, I made three quick upgrades to how Marie’s Brain works:.

    Then we re-ran the exact same six real-world SEO and AI Search questions – covering AI Overviews and traffic drops, whether to delete or rewrite informational posts, Main Content on commercial buyer’s guides, pruning thin location pages, agent readiness and /llms.txt, and a realistic five-hour-a-week plan that skips GEO distractions – across Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and Gemini 4 Neon.

    With the model names hidden and the columns randomized, I read all 18 answers and picked a winner on every prompt.

    When I hit reveal, the result wasn’t even close:.

    What stood out to me about Neon wasn’t that it had more facts – all three models pulled from the exact same OKF files. It was how it communicated. Neon’s answers felt more like a smart human thinking through a problem rather than a predictable AI response. I genuinely enjoyed reading them, and I immediately understood what they were trying to get across.

    My revealed blind test results (5/6 for Gemini 4 Neon), real Gemini API token usage, and pace-adjusted monthly cost estimates per user. Image Credit: Marie Haynes.

    Industry observers note that of course, better answers only matter if the economics make sense. Here are the real numbers from our live Concise-mode runs (using real Gemini API usageMetadata, including thinking tokens, at conservative uncached list rates):.

    Note on Neon’s speed: That 70.8s average was skewed by one single 3.5-minute API queue spike during testing; typical Neon replies ran 18 to 40 seconds (with text streaming on screen as it writes).

    Sources indicate that at first glance, $191 vs. $93 per 1,000 prompts sounds like a massive jump (about 10 cents extra per prompt). But when I mapped that against realistic full-month usage paces extrapolated from my early active users, here is what the extra cost per user looks like:.

    In a recent development, and those are conservative uncached estimates. Because every turn references the same ~55,000-token OKF Master Index, Gemini 4 Neon’s implicit context caching discounts repeated input tokens across multi-turn chats, bringing real-world bills noticeably lower.
